speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: USE OF ABRIDGED ORDER PAPER, DISTRIBUTION OF DAILY PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that during the last session an abridged version of the order paper was produced on an experimental basis. The primary purpose of the experiment was to reduce the very high cost of the printing of parliamentary publications without reducing the information provided to hon. members. After consultations with the house leaders of the various parties it appears that hon. members would agree that the abridged version of the order paper only should be published for a further experimental period. Should the short version prove unsatisfactory the regular version would be reintroduced.
Hon. members noticed, I am sure, the great volume of Hansards, order papers and other papers which accumulated under their desks in the past session. Following consultations with the several house leaders it has been agreed that the filing of such papers under members' desks could be discontinued. It is therefore proposed that the day-to-day papers and publications will continue to be placed on hon. members' desks but that those papers will be removed at the close of each day. An adequate supply of back issues in both languages will be maintained in both lobbies. The ordinary distribution to members' offices will continue as in the past.

I hope that hon. members will find such arrangements acceptable. I shall be pleased to receive suggestions and they will be given due consideration.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subsubtopic: ASSERTION OF CONTROL OVER ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Well, I could take some time to consider it, and in the meantime, if the hon. member would draw some lines on a map, they might help me.

subsubtopic: ASSERTION OF CONTROL OVER ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a further supplementary question to the Prime Minister. In. order to avoid any possibility of misunderstanding, am I to take it from what the Prime Minister said that Canada does claim jurisdiction and sovereign control over all the waters between the islands in the Canadian Arctic?

subsubtopic: ASSERTION OF CONTROL OVER ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the Leader of the Opposition is talking about the Canadian

Arctic, then I repeat, yes, we do exercise jurisdiction and we intend to exercise our sovereignty over that part of the world.

subsubtopic: ASSERTION OF CONTROL OVER ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: In order to avoid any misunderstanding, would the Prime Minister directly answer my question whether or not the government of Canada claims jurisdiction and is going to exercise jurisdiction over all the waters between the islands of the Canadian Arctic, for example, all the waters in the Canadian archipelago-the waters between the islands?

subsubtopic: ASSERTION OF CONTROL OVER ARCTIC WATERS

LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROGRESS TOWARD SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Labour. In view of the increasing impact on the British Columbia economy

resulting from the waterfront dispute in Vancouver, with an additional 2,400 employees being laid off today by one company in the forest industry, can the minister bring the house up to date and report on any progress made in his or departmental officials' discussions over the weekend with both parties to the dispute?

subtopic: LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROGRESS TOWARD SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday afternoon I met with representatives of the union's negotiating team and last night I met with the representatives of the BCMEA, the management organization. I shall have a further meeting today with the BCMEA. We have succeeded in clarifying the particular points in the proposed collective agreement to which the unions felt they had objection. I do not think the difficulties are insurmountable, and if progress were to continue today as rapidly as it did yesterday this strike could very well come to an end.
I am very pleased to answer the hon. member, who is so knowledgeable about labour aims, and I am sure he would be the last one in this House not to recognize that this strike could be settled tonight if the union were to ratify the agreement Which their negotiators thought desirable. If the hon. member is suggesting that I should bring in restrictive legislation, perhaps he could help me draft it, but in the meantime I am trying to settle the strike in the very near future by collective agreement.

subtopic: LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROGRESS TOWARD SETTLEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know why the minister suggested that I am recommending restrictive legislation because he knows I am not. That was a statement he made, not an answer to my question. As a supplementary question may I ask whether in the discussions he held with the union negotiating committee and the employers the point was raised that as the result of a subsequent dispute there might be a further hold-up caused by the threat of dispatchers to place picket lines around the port if they are not recognized as a collective bargaining unit?

subtopic: LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROGRESS TOWARD SETTLEMENT
speechtext: The answer is no, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to commence by doing what those who have preceded me in the debate have wisely and fairly done. I should like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address. I think each did a very excellent job in bringing his views to the attention of the House, and I sincerely add my congratulations to those that have already been expressed.
I was particularly interested in what the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) had to say when he devoted a great deal of his time to his ideas for speeding up the processes of parliament in order that we might be better able to handle the very large work load which is being piled higher and higher on parliament each year. All of us in this House, I think, would agree with what he said. Certainly I agree, and I spoke in this regard in the House last July 14.
At that time I outlined three steps which I suggested could be taken to speed up greatly the processes and the business of the House. This would cut down the time required by parliament to handle its business by no less than two-thirds. It would not in any way interfere with the democratic process of parliament or the rights of any member to express himself fully in the House.
After I concluded my speech on that occasion several Liberal members rose to speak. They agreed with what I had said. In fact, I do not know of anyone in parliament or any member of the press who disagreed with what I said or the suggestions I put forward, their practicability or their effectiveness.

Therefore it seems strange to me that a government which found it necessary to introduce the guillotine measure has shown no interest whatsoever in these measures.
The hon. member for Sarnia will get an answer when he talks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about his ideas. He will find out that the Prime Minister is simply not interested in speeding up the processes of parliament. The Prime Minister wants to control parliament. He wants to computerize parliament by putting legislation in at one end and having it come out on a certain date at the other end, exactly as he put it in, without being interfered with in any way by parliament. That is not the parliamentary process. This will be perhaps one of the first but not the last disappointments or disillu-sionments to be experienced by the hon. member for Sarnia in respect of both his Prime Minister and the government under which he serves.
On Friday we were treated to the Prime Minister's speech during which he took some time to describe the conditions endured by people in various parts of the country who are living today in poverty. However, there was not one word in his speech about any specific policy the government proposes to bring forward to deal with this very serious matter. In fact, his speech and the throne speech simply deal with this matter in pious platitudes of hope and general intent.
Let me remind the Prime Minister that the poor people of this country cannot eat pious platitudes; they cannot clothe themselves with pious platitudes and they cannot shelter themselves from the cold, the rain and the wind with pious platitudes. What they want is a cessation of task forces and cabinet committees such as those which have been sitting now for a year and a half without producing any visible results.
As a member of a former government I sat on many cabinet committees, and set up task forces. I have never known of a cabinet committee or a task force which, if properly set up and instructed by a minister, could not produce specific and good solutions well within a year. These task forces and cabinet committees are simply blinds covering inaction and the fact that this government does not know where it is going or where it intended to go when it promised on the hustings to produce a just society. The government had no idea how it would do this and today it still has no idea how it will do it.
October 27, 19G9

Why is it that the Prime Minister and the government are adopting a negative attitude toward this very important matter of poverty which the Prime Minister agreed was a national disgrace? The answer was given by no less a person than the former deputy Prime Minister, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), when he resigned a few months ago. He said very specifically that the Prime Minister was not interested in the ordinary problems facing the poor and less fortunate people of this country. He told us that the Prime Minister was really interested only in questions such as constitutional law, a subject he taught at the University of Montreal. This is a very important question, but I say to him that the people of this country cannot wait for the completion of his philosophical discussions before he attempts to deal with the practical problems now faced by the less fortunate people in Canada.
These are the people of Canada the Prime Minister said he was going to help when he created his just society. Let me invite the Prime Minister and the government to create this just society and bring the task forces and cabinet committees to a conclusion. Let them produce specific policies and then announce those policies to the House and to the country. Let us get on with the job of creating a just society and stop just talking about it.
We must not be too harsh on the Prime Minister about his speech because it was a rather gentle and platitudinous one which accomplished one very important thing. I should like to compliment him for that. It is well known that there are a number of members of the Prime Minister's party who suffer from insomnia. As the Prime Minister spoke, we on this side of the house could see that those gentlemen were gradually overcoming their malady. A strange silence and peace descended on the House like a blanket. Members of the press gallery quietly left, and parliament slept.

speechtext: Look at them now.

speechtext:
When parliament opened a year ago I spoke during the debate about this matter of poverty. That was on September 20th. The situation had been outlined by the Economic Council of Canada in its report published the previous month. At that time I asked the government to increase the federal minimum wage to compensate for the 13 per cent increase in the cost of living which had taken place since the federal minimum wage was last increased in July, 1965, some three
The Address-Mr. Hees and a half years ago. I suggested this as a first step toward overcoming what the council had described and the Prime Minister had agreed was a national disgrace.
During the past year the people of Canada have been treated to a number of very interesting performances on television. In each case the principal actor was that self-styled Babe Ruth of the bargaining table, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). He really is an awfully nice fellow, but he has succumbed to that which even athletes and other people suffer when they start to believe their own press notices. Unfortunately the minister has started to believe the great number of press releases he instructs his publicity people to issue on every possible occasion. It is nothing new for Canadians to see him before the television cameras.
On several of these occasions we heard the Minister of Labour announce that he was pleased to have been able to serve the strong and powerful unions which were in a position to cause the government great embarrassment through work stoppages. In any event he was pleased to have been able to assist them in coming to an agreement with their employers, and to announce increase in wages and fringe benefits of between 8 per cent to 11 per cent a year. This is just twice the increase that has taken place in the past year or so in the cost of living. During that same period and during the previous three years this government has done absolutely nothing to ease the situation of those living in poverty. In fact, during the past year the cost of living has gone up by another 5 per cent, making the situation of these unfortunate people that much worse.
[DOT] (12 Noon)
The Minister of Labour in Toronto recently said to certain press men-and it was published in the press-that he believed the minimum wage should be either $1.50 or $1.75 an hour. But have we seen any indication by this government that it intends to increase the minimum wage to any such figures? The answer is no. This wage has been increased for four and half years. Why? Simply because the people living on minimum wages today in all parts of Canada are, because of their lack of education, lack of health and lack of training, unorganized. They are not strong; they are not able to bring pressure to bear upon industry or the government and embarrass the government by a work stoppage. So the government pays absolutely no attention whatsover to them. It has allowed their cost of living to go up by no

October 27, 19G9
The Address-Mr. Hees less than 18 per cent during the past four and half years with no indication whatever that it intends to increase the minumum wage at this or any other time. It has become painfully obvious that the just society exists only for the strong, the well organized and those able to embarrass the government with a serious work stoppage.
As the government obviously has no intention of laying before parliament at this or any other session in the future a plan for ameliorating the very serious situation which faces those who live in poverty today, I intend at this time to present to parliament a plan which I think will be both practical and effective. First of all, let us ask ourselves, what is poverty and where it is to be found? We learn from the report of the Economic Council, which has become accepted as the authoritative study on this subject, that there are certain income levels which the council claims must be attained by the following categories of our citizens if those poeple are to live above the poverty level. These are the categories: single, with no dependants; single, with one or two dependants; married, with no children; married, with one, two, three, four or five children.
According to the report, the majority of the nearly five million people in Canada who live in poverty today work for the minimum wages set by the federal and provincial governments for the industries which come under their particular jurisdictions. These minimum wages vary between $1 and $1.30 an hour. The federal minimum wage today is $1.25 an hour. As I said earlier, this was raised last in July, 1965. At that time it raised the recipient's wages just above the poverty line. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics tells us that, in the intervening four and a half years, the cost of living has increased 18 per cent and has gone up by 5 per cent during the last 12 months. Therefore I believe it is obvious to everyone that if people receiving the federal minimum wage are to be able to provide a living for themselves and their families above the poverty level, we must raise that minimum wage now by at least 25 per cent.
Now let us have a look at such a raise from the viewpoint of the income standards set by the Economic Council of Canada. The Economic Council takes as its average family one with two dependent children, and says that if such a family is to live just above the poverty line it must receive an income of at least $3,500 a year. If a man receiving the federal minimum wage works a standard 40-hour week he earns $50 a week, and if he works
IMr. Hees.]
for the full year he earns $2,600 in that year. Because he has two dependent children he receives an additional $200 in family allowances during the year, which brings the total up to $2,800. Therefore, for this family to live above the poverty line, it is obvious that the breadwinner must earn an additional $700 during the year, or an increase of 25 per cent. Therefore I believe the first step in combating poverty in this country is for the federal government to raise the federal minimum wage by a minimum of 25 per cent.
The second step should be to call a federal-provincial conference to persuade the provinces to follow the lead given by the federal government. I believe that if the Prime Minister would point out the need for following the federal lead, both clearly and forcibly, and if the conference is given full television, press and radio coverage, the provincial premiers would find it very difficult, if not impossible, to refuse to follow the federal government's lead and would raise their minimum wages by a similar percentage. I think they would find it difficult, if not impossible, not to take this action whereby they would allow the people living under their jurisdictions, and working for minimum wages, to emerge above the poverty line.
I believe it is important that we realize that raising minimum wages would not increase federal or provincial expenditures by one penny, and therefore would not require any increase in taxes. It would simply require that employers who are paying poverty wages should pay a living wage which would enable their employees to live above the poverty line.
The third step in this fight against poverty, I believe, should be for the federal government to amend its present social security legislation, which discourages a recipient of social security from working at a part-time job to augment his or her assistance by reducing the payment by the amount the person earns from a part-time job. Those who receive pensions and other forms of assistance are kept from living in absolute want and privation by these pensions and assistance, but they are required to live below the poverty line because they are not allowed to supplement their pension or assistance by working at a part-time job.
The majority of those who receive social security benefits because of age, mental or physical disability, or inability to find a fulltime job, are able to work at a part-time job, and most of these people are anxious to do so.
October 27, 1969	COMMONS
For this reason,, 1 believe our social security legislation must be amended at this session to allow the recipients to earn the difference between their pension or allowance and the poverty level set by the Economic Council for their particular category. Once this poverty level has been reached, I believe the assistance can then be cut back at an increased rate as their income rises above the poverty line.
Many of those who receive social security because of age, disability, or some other reason, are unable to do even part-time work and will always be completely dependent upon the assistance they receive. These people really need help. The assistance we make available to them should be sufficient to enable them to live above the poverty line.
To make this possible, I believe our social security structure must be overhauled right away so that those who now are receiving an adequate income, and therefore do not need social security, should cease to receive it. In this way those who really need social security may receive adequate payments which would enable them to live above the poverty line. This would not require the imposition of the means test but could be done, both easily and painlessly, through income tax returns. Such a social security overhaul is long overdue, and should be started by the government without further delay.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
As a great deal of our social security legislation is within provincial jurisdiction, there is a great need to amend provincial legislation to permit part-time work to increase the income of those receiving social security at least to the poverty level. This matter should be discussed at the federal-provincial conference on poverty which the government should call, and the provinces should be urged to follow the lead of the federal government. Once again, I am convinced that a strong and logical presentation by the Prime Minister, together with full publicity by press, radio and television at the conference, will persuade the premiers that it makes good sense to amend their present social security legislation to permit those able to do part-time work to do so and thereby lift themselves out of the poverty cycle.
Finally, I would like to suggest some steps for the government to take to enable our farmers, our businessmen and our other producers to expand their production, and thereby increase the national income and make

The Address-Mr. Sullivan more good jobs available for our people, which is the only real social security. I believe that this can best be done by offering tax incentives to induce our producers to increase both their productivity and the industrial research which they either are, or should be, carrying out. I believe that this is the most effective way to enable our producers to lower their costs and turn out more new, attractive and lower priced products which will sell more readily against foreign competition both in the export market and here in Canada.
Such tax incentives, which we ail know are only paid after the desired results have been obtained, will pay for themselves many times over in the form of more income taxes, because there will be more people working and paying income tax rather than living on social security. May I say in conclusion that I believe that if the government will take the steps I have outlined, we can go a long way toward lifting our people out of the poverty in which so many of them have been forced to live for so long.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first extend my congratulations on the presentation of the throne speech which indicates we can expect a most interesting and, I hope, productive session. As indicated in the legislative outline, we shall again be considering format changes which will significantly influence the conduct of business in this House. Among the proposed changes I hope we shall find that members will be given the right to file speeches for the record without orally delivering them in the House. There is ample precedence for this step as this practice is now followed by, among others, the British House of Commons. There is an obvious saving in time and the purpose of the member as well as the official record are well served.
It is safe to say that every member of this House sought and accepted election with a view to serving his country by effectively representing his constituents. We came here believing that we could make a contribution. We came here believing that a parliament selected by the people should govern this country. We came here with the approval of the people. We came here not only prepared


The Address-Mr. Sullivan to listen to our constituents but expecting to find a forum wherein our constituents through us could and would be heard.
While casting about for ways and means to make this contribution we, first year members, have made some remarkable discoveries. All too often parliament does not govern this country. All too often members, regardless of their dedication, are expected to be seen but not heard. We are asked to listen to the nation but we are seldom asked to tell anyone what we have heard. The fault lies with the members of this House.
Under the present system-and this is true no matter what party is in power-a backbench member of the government, because of the party discipline, is expected to vote with his party regardless of his researched opinion. His integrity may well have to be compromised. Only in exceptional circumstances is this practice not followed. It is true that under the present system there is ample opportunity for discussion and consultation. However, after this consultation and discussion, if a government member cannot agree with the government's proposal he is nevertheless expected to vote in favour of that proposal. Why? Because of party discipline. It is absolutely necessary that there be party discipline for the party to operate under our system; our system is completely dependent upon party discipline.
I suggest, first, that there is the possibility that under our present system a cabinet minister could become a captive of the civil service. There is a further possibility that the civil servants, not being responsible to the people or to Members of Parliament, could formulate the policies which could result in the adoption of these policies by the government.
I suggest also that much of the talent in this House is being wasted under our present committee system. For some reason, almost unbelievable in the modern concept of efficiency, members are assigned to a large number of committees dealing with very complex and diverse subject matters and are expected to absorb enough to make a meaningful contribution at the committee level. I submit that we cannot even read, never mind research, all the evidence before all the committees upon which we are asked to serve. The result does not even reach the level of knowing a little bit about a lot of things; it stops somewhere near the area of being quite thoroughly confused about nearly everything. Some members have avoided this particular trap by concentrating on one or two subjects or


committees and merely giving lip service to the balance of their committee assignments.
Systems are allowed to develop, but if they do not serve the intended purpose those operating within the system must bear the responsibility for the deficiencies or shortcomings. There is an old homily that says: "Grant us the courage to change those things which can be changed, the strength to accept those things which cannot be changed, and wisdom enough to tell the difference." I take those words as good advice and most applicable to any discussion of rules changes or governmental reform as it applies to this House.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
As a new member of the House, and as a government backbencher, I have come to appreciate the effort made by the government to include all the members of all parties in the decision-making process. As I see the cumbersome nature of this process, even the improved model, it is easy to understand the frustration of earlier parliamentarians, the sometimes annoyance of present members, and the impatience of those we represent.
This House has occasionally taken steps to improve its methods of conducting business, legislative or otherwise, and has even made motions toward striking a more presentable listening pose for the benefit of our constituents. Such change is admirable, and is indeed necessary if this institution is to remain a viable force or even a reasonable influence within a rapidly changing society. It is ironical, therefore, that each step, no matter how timorous, is greeted with bleats of delight by the reformers on the one hand, and with charges of creeping republicanism on the other.
During the last federal campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) summed up participation with these words:
No man alone and no party, even a majority party, can solve these problems if it does not constantly have recourse to the people, if it does not constantly involve the people, not always in the solution of these problems, but in the examination of them.
This recourse to the people is the basic, in fact, the only justifiable reason for even having an elected Member of Parliament. Recourse to the people is the aim and the purpose of better research facilities, regional desks and expanded committee involvement. As two students of political science, Mr. Ian McConachie and Miss Susan Jones, have said, "The ultimate goal is government which is not only responsible but responsive." The


steps taken by the present government have assisted us toward this goal but the steps already taken are, I hope, only a beginning.
There can be no true recourse to the people until such time as each member of this House is better able to reflect the views and positions of his own constituents. This can only become a fact when each member of this House can, in conscience, submerge his concern over the fall of the government and turn his mind directly to the issue at hand and its effect on his people. He must be allowed to bring his acquired insights back here and be heard.
Consideration must be given to a form of government where the executive branch presents its legislative program statute by statute; then after full discussion on all possible amendments the matter is voted upon and, if the proposal brought in by the executive branch is not passed, the government should not fall. I am one who believes that the executive branch is not always correct. I am one who believes in a system that permits the elected Members of Parliament to have the obligation to assume the responsibility of forming their own opinion in the last analysis and of voting accordingly. Surely this is what the electors in our constituencies want us to do.
I propose that there should be a fixed term of government. I propose that election to the office of Prime Minister should come by popular vote. In my opinion we should establish an executive branch of government which is independent of the legislative branch and not responsible to it.
In my opinion the legislative branch should not be under the discipline of the executive branch of any government. We have already come close to acknowledging the existence of an executive branch but we just refuse to accept the responsibility of control. Call it galloping republicanism if you will, but if it might mean more effective or more representative government it should not be rejected simply because it is new to us here in Canada.
I know there are difficulties and disadvantages to such a system but these, to my mind, are outweighed by the greater flexibility afforded by such a change. For example, government by department or government by the civil service would be greatly curtailed and the temptation to dictate, which must sometimes be very real, would be eliminated. The power and the control would be diffused not 21362-8
The Address-Mr. Sullivan only throughout the government side but throughout this House.
As a further example the Prime Minister, as head of the executive branch of such a government, could select his subaltern executives from either within the membership of the House or beyond, if he should so desire. There are many circumstances under which a Prime Minister could reach to those who could not or would not dedicate themselves to a political career and invite these special talents to head government departments without joining the civil service.
I suggest that the public and this House would be better served if the need to give lip service were eliminated and members were assigned to one committee only and thereby given an opportunity to become expert in this assigned or selected field. The result would be smaller committees, more thorough examination of proposals and views at the committee stage, and a more direct contribution to resulting legislation. The great advantage would be the emergence of Members of Parliament who are at least equally expert as the civil servants upon whom we now must depend so heavily.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that some of the changes I have described could be made through legislation which will come before us during this new session. Other changes will require further consideration, but such consideration should take on a greater air of urgency at the hands of the existing standing committees.
I would like to make it clear that in my proposals there would be no change in the status of Her Majesty the Queen in relation to the people of Canada, and that we remain firmly committed as members of the Commonwealth.
Change is always fraught with some difficulty and can seldom even be described as comfortable, but it is necessary. It is especially necessary if we ever hope to have the members of this House speak for the people and really "tell it the way it is."
No matter how much some of those who have been members of this House for a long period of years would like to cling to an out-of-date system, these proposals will bring the people more in touch with legislation, would be a truer form of democracy and, in my opinion, a more satisfactory form of democracy for Canada. This must be our prime consideration. As the member from Sarnia in his speech said so well, "Canada must come first."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my congratulations to those offered by other hon. members to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It was apparent to all of us that they had a great awareness of the current problems facing the country. I also wish to congratulate the hon. member who preceded me. I must say I am in sympathy with a great many of the views he expressed. I believe we should do more thinking along the lines he suggested.
The Speech from the Throne espoused many laudable aims. It would be difficult for anyone to disagree with many portions of it, and if its intentions are carried out with integrity and fairness this Canada of our's will be a better place in which to live.
However, so many of the urgent issues of the day were omitted from the Speech from the Throne that it is very difficult to speak to that document and still remain relevant to the state of the nation as it really exists. Take, for instance, the tremendous national problem of Canada's agricultural industry. I speak now of the whole industry from coast to coast and not just of western wheat production. All that is to be found in the Speech from the Throne on this problem is a suggestion that a crisis indeed does exist in relation to wheat sales, and that Parliament will be asked to consider some amendments to the Canada Grain Act. This is equivalent to tackling a blazing barn with a cup of water. What Canadians have a right to expect from the government is recognition that one of this nation's great resource industries is in desperate need of fundamental overhaul and that speedy and comprehensive action must be forthcoming or there will be a disaster.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
If anyone doubts that I speak only for the western farmer let him consult the potato grower in the Maritimes, the dairy farmer in Ontario and Quebec or the mixed farmer in British Columbia. And if anyone doubts the national aspect of wheat production on the prairies let him consider the market where the agricultural machinery manufacturer of central Canada sells his product, where the automobile manufacturer of central Canada sells his cars, where the appliance maker, the tool marker, the steel fabricator and all the other makers of goods and services, largely concentrated elsewhere in Canada than the west, sell their products. Let him ask the railway worker, the trucker, the elevator worker, the longshoreman and the seaman,

not to mention the broker, the clerk and all the service businesses attached to those involved in moving grain across this country, how they are affected.
As an example I have here a few figures on recent sales of farm machinery in the west and the lay-offs among skilled Ontario workers that the cut-back in these sales has brought. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics' figures indicate that sales of farm equipment in 1968 declined 14 per cent from those of 1967. Figures for the first five months of 1969 show that sales of new farm equipment in the prairie provinces declined a further 17.2 per cent from 1968.
I have here a request by the Saskatchewan Implement Dealers Association in relation to the situation in the west that I would like to read:
The seriousness of the western situation is illustrated by a recent request from the Saskatchewan Implement Dealers Association that farm equipment manufacturers set up moratoriums on the interest payments dealers must make to manufacturers for new farm equipment.
The association says that, if dealers are required to pay interest ranging from 10 per cent to 14 per cent on new machinery in their lots, 50 per cent of its 450 members will be forced out of business this year.
The dealers receive farm machinery from the manufacturers on a past-due note and assume money from machinery sales in the summer can be used to pay off the note when it falls due.
But this year, with new machinery sales in Saskatchewan down 30 per cent to 50 per cent, the dealers must pay interest for machines they still have not sold.
"The present cash shortage of farms and the resulting reduction in new farm machinery sales will create a marked and serious decline in the number of farm equipment dealers," Richard Jensen, president of the association, says.
Leo King, secretary-manager of the association, says if manufacturers do not suspend the required interest payments the dealers will ask the provincial government to pass legislation setting up moratoriums.
If this service is to be continued in the west, help must soon be forthcoming. Machine sales figures do not tell the whole story inasmuch as dealers, besides increased inventories, are carrying two or three times as much in overdue accounts as they ever have before. This applies not only to machine dealers but to all businessmen operating in agricultural areas at this time.
The figures for International Harvester show that profits were down in 1968 from 1967 by something like 30 per cent in the western farm equipment area. Average employment in the International Harvester

plant in Ontario was down by 1,000 in 1968 from 1967 and the cuts are liable to be much worse when the 1969 figures are complete. Last week Massey-Ferguson laid off 250 men. The Cockshutt division of the White Motor Company has closed its combine plant for three months with a lay-off of 450 men. This is all in the industrial heart of Canada, right here in Ontario. During the summer Massey-Ferguson extended the vacation period for something like a month, affecting 1,200 employees, because of slow sales. The only reason the disastrous agricultural situation has not had a more adverse effect on our whole national industrial complex is the nullifying effect of our industry in many areas producing to near capacity for the U.S. military machine. But this situation will not continue too much longer.
The problem of wheat production was brushed aside with a few lines in the Speech from the Throne. The government has been well aware of the situation for more than a year and a half. It has sent out task forces, had surveys made and even had the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) take a first-hand look at the situation. So far the only action has been criticism and advice-criticism of the farmer for growing so much of a product no longer in high demand and advice to diversify.
This may be the answer, but to carry it out will require massive government assistance, expert technical advice and a follow-through by way of helping to establish new markets. It will require massive financial assistance to carry out the necessary capital expenditures involved in this change. A grain-producing plant cannot lightly or easily be switched to producing another crop any more than a plant manufacturing tanks can be cheaply or easily retooled to produce motor cars, tractors or brassieres.
The Canadian farmer and the Canadian agricultural community deserve much better from this government than a supercilious nod, and this, I say, is all that the Speech from the Throne gave in this area of agriculture.

speechtext:
The Speech from the Throne acknowledged that pollution is a problem and that something must be done. But the implication this government has always left when talking about pollution is that industry is the principal offender. My suggestion to the
103
The Address-Mr. Downey government is that it should set an example in pullution control, as it claims to have done in austerity, by attending to its own backyard before pointing a finger at its neighbours. One has but to go to the national park at Banff to see an example of this attitude of "Don't do as I do, do as I say." There an establishment directly under the control of the federal government continues to dump raw sewage into the Bow River. What sort of basis is that for discussions with provincial administrations designed to make a co-ordinated attack on pollution?
It was interesting to hear that the government sets so much store by the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion and that the sky is the limit there. Austerity is not to be applied to that department's budget. This is all very fine if the public moneys to be spent on overcoming regional disparity are spent fairly and equitably. But I become suspicious when I see that my riding in central Alberta is excluded from the designated area and the Liberal riding that happens to be represented by the Minister of Agriculture is included. So far as the need for new industry and regional economic expansion is concerned, both ridings are identical. Decisions such as this tend to cast some doubt cn the integrity of the whole program.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Even greater doubt arises from the announced priorities within the area designated for expansion. As I recall it, these priorities list Quebec, the Maritimes and Manitoba in that order, with the rest trailing a poor fourth. I suggest to the government that they should take another long look at the area designated, with a view to expanding it to take in areas that stand in equal need of industrial assistance. They could well expand to include areas that lie beyond the immediate area of the large, booming metropolitan areas.
The list of issues barely mentioned or passed over completely in the government's legislative program as outlined in the Speech from the Throne is almost endless. For example, consider the question of pensions. So far the government has paid only lip service to the multiple recommendations contained in the Woods Report. It is true that they have done something for the Hong Kong veterans, but they have made only a token gesture or no gesture at all in other important areas. The old age pensioners and retired federal public servants have been ignored and left to

The Address-Mr. Downey be crushed between their pitifully low fixed incomes and the steadily rising cost of living. It seems to me that the time is long past for some method of providing an automatic supplement to enable the fixed incomes of old and retired people to meet the bare necessities of life in a supposedly affluent society. Present automatic increases being considered in this area are hardly realistic. I have heard our society described as both affluent and just, but there seems to be evidence that the contrary is true.
The newspapers have been filled with stories about the Company of Young Canadians being a hotbed of seditious activity and about their having links with subversive and terrorist organizations round the world. The front pages have been covered with headlines about the French network of the CBC being controlled by separatists. Indeed, the Prime Minister himself was pictured throwing down the gauntlet to separatists and advising the English element in Quebec to get out, compete, and not allow themselves to be stepped on. Yet there is no hint of these problems in the Speech from the Throne.
I must confess that I was puzzled by the Prime Minister's advice to English speaking Quebeckers. When he said "compete", he did not say how. Should they make larger bombs? Should they take to the streets with bigger and better riots and overturn statues in Quebec? What did the Prime Minister mean when he said "compete"? After all, in a society of violence one can only compete by resorting to even greater violence.
As to the Company of Young Canadians, my solution to the problem is quite simple: abolish the outfit. This would be, to my mind, an admirable economy measure as well as a step toward restoring tranquility in areas of trouble.
The Prime Minister has indicated that he will no longer tolerate violence and lawlessness in this country. This matter must surely be of great concern to him as we cannot help but note that the forces of crime and anarchy in this country have blossomed well during his time in office. That charge, however, is true not only of Canada. The lawmakers of this nation have been so obsessed with human rights that we have ended up with a definite xrend that supports the criminal element instead of supporting a victimized society. Our police have their hands tied in this legal jungle. Crime is one of the largest businesses in the country today. Criminals have the

money to hire the best brains and to develop and use the best systems devised by education and science. We send our law enforcement agencies against them with one hand tied behind their backs. Our law enforcement agencies cannot use the latest and best techniques because that might infringe on somebody's rights. There is even talk in some areas of the country of taking away the guns from our policemen. Our police are not supposed to shoot until they are shot at. They are supposed to take verbal abuse, sticks, stones and the like, and if some rioters lose a little blood our police may be hauled into our courts and the hue and cry of police brutality goes up.
What a mockery we are making of our law enforcement agencies. To be a policeman today you have to be either a damned fool or damned dedicated. From a practical standpoint the rioter and looter have more rights than has the storekeeper, whose rights are infringed upon. The murderer or criminal who beats and robs honest citizens has more rights than has the policeman who might injure the criminal in the course of subduing him and taking him to the station.
In this vast penal hotel system that we have in Canada, with its central heating, television, recreation and balanced diets, it is more of a penalty to be on the outside and have to put up with taxes, pollution, traffic jams and bill collectors. It is more of a penalty to be on the outside looking in. I see that now we are considering letting the girls in with the boys in our penitentiaries. After a few years our criminals will be beating down the doors to get into one of these educational paradises of crime. What we need in this country are shorter and fewer prison sentences but much more access to the bullwhip and the rock pile, and a few hangings thrown in. I do not think that would be too much. Dignity of the individual seems to apply only to criminals. For the law-abiding citizen or the policeman, there is little dignity in the rapes, beatings and murders that we see in this country today.
Another subject much in the national news is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Many Canadians appear to be perennially unhappy with the performance of this taxeating monster. Instead of closing down one of its services, reducing its funds or firing employees, why not put it to some national purpose?
Everyone by now is familiar with the crowded universities of this country where

bodies of students ranging from 10,000 to
20,000	no longer permit personal attention in teaching. We seem to see nothing except a mass production technique. A body goes in one end with a high school certificate and comes out of the other with a degree. It seems to me that the CBC could be utilized to provide lectures every bit as personal as those now available in most of our universities. The corporation could be converted into a single, huge, national university at least for instructional purposes. This step might help to solve the grave problems of overcrowding, student financing and expensive facilities, and bring into the national educational net many fine young brains now unable, for one reason or another, to acquire a higher education.
Another matter which I was disappointed to see omitted in the Speech from the Throne deserves to be mentioned. I am speaking of our national oil policy which, of course, is in serious danger. May I now read some comments made by the president of the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada who, in an address on October 11, 1969, said:
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Refinery expansion in Ontario has not kept pace with growing needs in that province, imports are now coming in from further east and will grow in volume simply because no refining capacity is under construction. A proposed 100,000 barrels daily refinery for the Toronto-Hamilton area, dedicated to Canadian oil, can't yet start because of local opposition to zoning for a $100,000,000 plant. The plant, when finally site is approved, will take two years to build. It would apparently have no federal or provincial tax concessions to help it compete.
Yet, in Quebec and the Maritimes, massive refinery construction has begun or has been given clearance that would raise capacity by several hundred thousand barrels daily, far in excess of needs of the Canadian markets served by overseas oil. Result will inevitably be new harsh pressures on markets for oil produced in Canada. AH of these refineries have been given either provincial or federal tax benefits, or grants in aid. One, on which construction has started in Newfoundland, was recently granted by federal Order in Council a 100 per cent capital cost allowance which gives it substantial advantage over other refineries.
1 have no quarrel with government assistance to upgrade the economies of less favoured regions in Canada-but can the concept of aid justify excessive construction of one type of manufacturing plant, to be subsidized by all Canadians whose local benefits will be far less than the burden they will impose on the over-all economy, reducing markets for Canadian production, and increasing the foreign exchange burden of oil imports?
An even more serious defect in present Canadian oil policy is the ignoring of the vital question, security of supply. Canada, in effect, assumes that foreign oil will always be available, at low cost and in adequate quantity, even if emergencies occur; at least until such time as domestic oil from
The Address-Mr. Danson
the Atlantic basin or the far north becomes available, hopefully in a few years. The assumption is dangerous, for it fails to take into account the trends of oil supply and demand affecting the major sources of eastern Canada's emergency supplies; and the rising insecurity of oil originating in the Arab nations of the Middle East and Africa.
Again I say we must review the entire matter of oil policy in the coming year.

speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, before I was so politely interrupted just before lunch, the policy of the government in presenting white papers and policy papers represents a departure which I believe has considerable merit. It is very disturbing. It is disturbing to us as members of the house and it is disturbing to the public because it has a tendency to make us think. It disturbs us. We shall be getting a lot of mail from people who are upset, and those of us who serve on committees will be holding long hearings and listening to the views of interested parties and
[Mr. Danson.1

groups from across the country. It is an interesting process. When we realize what is really happening I think we shall be pleased, indeed, because the whole nation is being allowed to participate in the legislation which is finally passed by this house. I am not quite sure it is good politics, since it upsets people so, but I am convinced it is darned good government and very good for democracy.
We shall see this borne out most clearly, I think, when we come to consider the white paper on tax reform which is to come before the committee upon which I sit. No one really likes to see tax changes. They affect us all in one way or another; we all tend to think that the right taxes are those which the other fellow pays. Nevertheless, we must all carry our burden in this respect, and, realizing this, we fear a change; we prefer the devil we know to the devil we don't know. But if we really believe in this country of ours, if we really want to see a united Canada, as we say, if we really want to cure regional disparities, to do something about pollution and so on, we had better be prepared to put our money where our mouth is, in a fair and equitable way. I hope and believe that this is what the proposed reforms outlined in the white paper on the tax structure will do.
I enjoyed listening to the speeches of the leaders of the opposition parties in the house on Friday. It was entertaining, indeed though a little sad, too. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is a good man, a responsible man and a man respected greatly by everyone in this house-no more so than by myself. He criticized our priorities, as he should, and as do we on this side of the house. But decisions have to be made; everything cannot be done at once, and there is so much to be done. He criticized our policy in relation to inflation, but as far as I can see he proposed no viable alternatives. The leader of the New Democratic party also criticized us on this score. I must say I did not stay for the whole of the speech made by the leader of the Creditistes (Mr. Caouette). I believed I had heard it before-that I could go back through Hansard and find it all set out there as reported in earlier years. It was something like a manifesto from Marx-Groucho Marx. The leader of the New Democratic party dealt with inflation, and talked about the slack in our economy. When I heard his proposals, his solutions, I realized that he had been caught with his slacks down. He listed government expenditures which were supposed to be contributing
October 27, 1969	COMMONS
to inflation but I noticed that only one of them had been incurred by the 28th parliament.
He listed a number of solutions, such as increased pensions, guaranteed incomes and expenditure to remove regional disparities- which we are presently making-but all of these proposals really do not affect the challenge presently facing us; I really do not believe they have any bearing on inflation whatever. Then, of course, he talked about anti-ballistic missiles, because they come in everywhere, and he once again outlined proposals for dealing with the effects of foreign ownership. In this regard, I find myself in agreement with some of the points he made. He went on to make mention of the advantages of a floating exchange rate, but before long he floated off across the horizon where I was disinclined to follow him. He quoted the sixth report of the Economic Council, criticizing the government for not following its recommendations, but he made no reference to the testimony given before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs by Professor Neufeld of the University of Toronto or by Governor Rasminsky of the Bank of Canada who put forward proposals inconsistent with those contained in the economic review-proposals which are consistent with government policy. And government policy in this regard seems to be taking effect at the present time.
* (2:10 p.m.)
I do not think even the N.D.P. members of the committee, with all their simplicity, would accept the simplistic distortions presented in this House on Friday. I am fairly sure they are embarrassed as a matter of fact, because this is the sort of irresponsible fudging of issues that misleads the uninformed they pretend to represent so ably.
The leader of the N.D.P. did, however, mention the increases in the price of steel. His party feels it is all right to raise wages but that these increases should not be reflected in prices. They say that wage increases should be absorbed by productivity increases, not realizing or not admitting that productivity comes not only from dedicated and skilled workers but from skilled management and from profits which are intelligently re-invested in most efficient plants to keep abreast of new technology.
Labour groups regrettably have refused to co-operate with the Prices and Incomes Commission. To date they have been stalling
DEBATES	107
The Address-Mr. Danson about appearing before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, which is studying interest rates and inflation. I do hope they will appear before our sittings are ended.
For some reason I fear their leaders, with all their easy criticisms and pat answers, are afraid to be exposed to their own membership -the hard-working union members-who, I am sure, are just as anxious to reduce inflation as any other group in this country. There is absolutely no value to a steel worker's pay increase when it results in a further inflationary spiral which negates the increase won after hard weeks on the picket line. Furthermore, an inflationary spiral of this type hits the very vulnerable, unorganized worker and, worse still, the defenseless pensioner, the unemployed, the handicapped and the aged whom the hon. members of the N.D.P. selfrighteously pretend to champion and for whom they almost drown us in crocodile tears. This is irresponsibility, I suggest, of the most cruel type.
As a concerned Canadian, I am fearful about the chain reaction the announced steel price increases can produce. The steel industry in Canada is cne of the best managed and most productive in our economy. It pays high wages, as high or higher than those south of the border; it is competitive even on the export markets, is as technically advanced as that anywhere, is profitable and pays dividends. It is also largely Canadian owned, which is an interesting fact. Its decisions are reached in Canada, in its own selfinterest, which is also Canadian self-interest. Its research and production facilities are oriented toward our resources and our markets and are eminently successful.
It is because of this success that I appeal to all segments of the steel industry to pause and to continue to show responsibility in the national interest. There is now talk about further increases in the prices of cars, always a direct consequence of steel price increases. Even the Ontario Hydro is using increased steel costs as an excuse to raise electric rates because of the large quantities of steel used in thermal plants. The results of this increase will undoubtedly spread to other sectors of the consumer durables field which has had a remarkable record of price stability over the past decade. Other manufacturers will follow suit.
It is critical to the success of our increasingly effective anti-inflation policies that the


The Address-Mr. Danson line be held, and held firmly. I appeal to the steel companies to take a position of unprecedented leadership at this time and rescind or moderate their announced increases, at least until the present measures in our fight against inflation begin to have a greater moderating effect on our economy. Then, hopefully, they will be less necessary. This will not be easy, but easy measures will not cure our present problems.
If some increases appear to be unavoidable I would urge the steel companies to sit down with government and labour, perhaps with the Prices and Incomes Commission, to negotiate any essential increases. This course will call for a degree of courage and responsibility of the very highest order, but if no one has anything to hide or fear, they could do themselves and all Canadians a great service indeed. Such an initiative could be the key factor, in addition to continuing government restraint, in breaking the back of the cancerous inflation psychology.
This action could also immediately and firmly establish the Prices and Incomes Commission as a truly effective instrument that could attack other areas of danger, most importantly the exploding services sector of our economy which now accounts for some 70 per cent of our gross national product. This is an area that is difficult to nail down and one to which we have been paying all too little attention.
As I mentioned before, there is disagreement sometimes about our priorities, and even disagreement within our party. In many cases I do not agree, but if we waited for unanimous agreement nothing would be accomplished. Nevertheless, from my orientation, I do not believe we are giving sufficient priority to the question of urban problems, a neglect that could well come back to haunt us. Canada is now 70 per cent urban, and in the 1980's it is predicted it will be 80 per cent urban. By the end of the century, it will be 90 per cent urban. In the urban area of greater metropolitan Toronto, from which I come, we have some 10 per cent of the population and almost 10 per cent of the membership of this house, with some 17 per cent of the membership in our party which sits over here. This is only one of the great urban areas of our nation.
My constituency of York North is especially affected. It sits on the northern edge of Toronto, although some of it is projected into the Metro area. We cannot isolate ourselves
[Mr. Danson.l
from Toronto anymore than the general Toronto region can isolate itself from other regions of the country. What happens in Cape Breton, Rimouski, the Indian Lake area of Manitoba, the Arctic or Roberts Bank is our concern. We are blessed in our region. We have expansion going on daily that would create headlines anywhere else. This hardly ruffles the surface. It is almost routine. I have in mind a 4,000 man increase in employment in one aircraft plant, of which most people in the area are not even aware, which puts additional pressure on the economy of our region. There was a $32 million development in one corner of my riding about which I read in the local suburban newspaper. So, we enjoy success and prosperity beyond measure. This prosperity results only because we are part of Canada and it will not be sustained if all regions of Canada are not prosperous. By the same token, we have very serious problems just as the wheat farmer in the west and the fisherman in Newfoundland have. If they are not prosperous we are not prosperous. Their concern has become our concern.
We can leam from problems in the United States. We can learn about those problems we might anticipate in our own urban centres. We are not immune to them. We have seen indications of these problems in one of our largest metropolitan areas. These problems are accelerating. They must be anticipated and handled. There are economic and social pressures. Living in the biggest city in the country is not necessarily, for me, living in the best. Our region is big enough, with a viable economy and all the important things that make it possible to have a good life, but it could be so much better. It will grow of its own volition without force feeding. We in the Toronto region have a responsibility. Without being parochial we will fight for that which effects us. We ask for your support in fighting these problems we think we must be solved now.
We are delighted with the appointment of a new cabinet member from our part of the country. He is a man with integrity and ability, a man of whom we are indeed proud. We from the greater Toronto area will be diligent in looking after the interests of our region and we ask for your support in this regard. We will not be parochial but we have a responsibility which we intend to assert, and we are asking for the support of our cabinet ministers in this regard to an extent not heretofore forthcoming.

The talk of expanding the metro region of Toronto to the townships of Markham and Vaughan, the largest geographic section of my constituency which as I said is on the northern fringe, could be the thin edge of the wedge in the formation of an uncontrolled megolopolis. This situation is not really very far away. What will happen to the towns in this constituency of mine like Markham, Unionville, Richmond Hill, Woodbridge and Thornhill which have their own identity and their own community spirit. In addition, they are semirural in their surroundings. What of the villages of Maple and Gormley? I am concerned because we might end up with solid concrete right from Lake Ontario to Lake Simcoe and then we would be faced with problems of transportation and pollution such as we never thought possible. However, these problems are predictable and they will put pressures on the economy of this region which will add to the inflationary pressures.
I suggest that the cost of planning and for the services necessary will be insignificant compared to the cost of neglecting this planning. The cost is incalculable in human terms but I think it is really quite calculable in economic terms. The long term economic and social advantages I believe can at least be equated with the regional economic expansion program, so we must weigh these priorities. The priority at the moment is in terms of regional economic expansion. This, I think, is an excellent program but I hope it does not mean we have to exclude attention to our urban areas. If the sixth review of the Economic Council, to which I referred earlier, tells us anything it tells us that we have much going for us in this country, that our potential is so great, our incomes will increase 50 per cent, I believe, by 1985 and we will have a 30 per cent increase in our standard of living. The Economic Council said all these things are ours "if", and then it listed a lot of things which really in essence boils down to, if we are not stupid, and there are no guarantees of that.
Neglect of urban areas and of the urban fact could be considered stupid. I think we
must watch this possibility and deal with it soon. So far as answers are concerned, I do not have the answers. Nothing is certain. I have suggestions, I have viewpoints and I have ideas. The experts in this field have proposals. We cannot be certain of anything but we can be certain that if we wait for absolute assured success, nothing will be done. If we do nothing, chaos is certain. The problems have been greatly aggravated by the neglect of the provinces' rightful responsibility in this field. This brings us back to our constitutional problems. There is a lack of communication between the federal level and the great urban municipalities of this country. In our province of Ontario, the government refuses to bring the Metro Toronto region and the municipal governments into consultations respecting matters directly affecting them. We are making decisions affecting airports around Toronto without consulting the metropolitan Toronto authorities. The provincial government will not let us get through to them.
In the provincial government, there is a minister of everything. He is the minister of just about anything one could name. He has announced a harbour city on Toronto island without consulting the Toronto people. Sure, he comes from Toronto or thereabouts, but this is arrogance of the worst kind. I think this must stop because we cannot accept it. I suggest that we seriously consider establishing a national institute of urban planning or perhaps urban and transportation planning because I think the two are closely interrelated. There is in the United States a committee, the national committee of urban growth and development, which serves this purpose. Such an institute could be associated with our universities, which could have excellent schools of urban and transportation studies. We would have the benefit of expertise there which would not be readily available to the government. Also, we would be training the people in universities to man the urban mechanisms that would be developed as a result. At the federal level, I could envisage Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation being represented as well as the Department of Transport, the Canadian Transport Commission or possibly the Department of Communications which would be vital.
Then, there are the concerns of provincial bodies such as housing, transport and the municipal boards. Most important, the urban centres themselves would be represented, the major urban centres per se, and the Canadian
110	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Danson Council of Mayors and. Municipalities. They should be part of the participating groups within such an institute. We are facing an awakening in our municipalities with the introduction of political parties into municipal politics. It is rather interesting that, for the first time, our party has selected as a mayoralty candidate a young man, a professor of political science of the University of Toronto, who everybody thought was a quiet academic from nowhere. He has come forth with the most thoughtful proposals that have ever been put forth in a municipal election in the history of our city. I think the voters of Toronto are beginning to wake up and realize that intelligent people and intelligent proposals are not excluded from municipal government and that there will be responsibility with a responsible party which will have a program. There is some hope now that action will be taken instead of everybody running off like scorpions, doing their own thing. You try to keep away from them and they try to keep away from you, but if you get near them they bite you.
With a responsible, well-led municipal political party I think we can make great strides in our large urban areas. As I said, the problems are certain. Many of them axe actually predictable. We have the opportunity and the responsibility, I believe, to plan and anticipate. "Anticipate" is my favourite word.
I believe in participatory democracy but I like anticipatory democracy better. In this way we can make decisions for future generations and many decisions for sane development of our urban centres. But if we fail, and if we hesitate or if we are shortsighted or, worse still, blind, future generations could well look back on us not as the just society but as the irresponsible society.
There are other priorities, but there is a long range priority about which I should like to speak which would divide our energies in two directions. One is to the senior citizens, the older people of this country, the people who are vulnerable and have no one speaking for them. There certainly are exceptions in this Home. I do not say that anyone is unconcerned, but really the fear people face in their old age is something that cannot be imagined, except by many of us who have lived with it in one form or another. This problem will affect us.
I think we should establish a system in which we make certain there is security and dignity in old age. We do this for very selfish

DEBATES	October 27, 1969
reasons. The most selfish reason is that there is nothing in it for us; it is just a good thing to do and makes us feel good. This is a sign of maturity. They do this much better than we do in what we consider to be less sophisticated societies. Another reason for action in this area is that with some degree of luck, we, too, will be old. I do not mean that the future should be looked after to such an extent that we just live for today and discourage savings to supplement whatever we do as a society for our senior citizens. However, our system should mean that we do not have to fear living with children in a garret or in homes for the aged which are undesirable. Fortunately, many of these homes for the aged are becoming more desirable but as yet there are not enough of them. We should look to the present and future, and direct our energies to those things which are productive, so that we use our . productive years productively.
We in this House have really awesome responsibilities to the people of this country. We may make mistakes. We will not solve all the problems, and when we solve some there will be new ones that we did not dream existed. In making mistakes, we will be criticized by the new generation but the members of the new generation will make their share of mistakes, too. However, they know a great deal more than we did at the same age and they are picking out our mistakes a lot more easily. We will not do everything, but we must not be guilty of not trying.

speechtext:
It is
with pleasure that I rise to participate in the throne speech debate. My first words will be to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau). They both spoke well and in a spirit of sincerity and frankness which does credit to the constituencies which elected them to this house.
I also wish to congratulate the two new ministers without portfolio and the two new parliamentary secretaries. There is no question about the fact that the appointments were made to well deserving members but, quite frankly, there are mounting doubts among many Canadians about the over-all capacity of this cabinet to deal with Canada's problems.
I have read and re-read the throne speech searching for the key which will open the


door to the fulfillment of the promise of a just society, but I have searched in vain. The throne speech reminds me somewhat of the eye of a tornado which is almost still, almost without motion, while the destructive gale force winds whirl ever faster and faster until they form a cone between heaven and earth which destroys everything that comes in its path.
By its inaction and indecision, this government is permitting the winds of division and inflation to destroy our economy. These are not my views alone; they are endorsed in very brief words in today's editorial in the Financial Times which read as follows:
.. .the objectives of the legislative program are reasonably clear, but there is still a good deal of mystery surrounding the means.
I cannot understand the apathy of this government. Its pious platitudes about the state of the nation, as indicated in the throne speech, show that the present Liberal cabinet is living in an ivory tower, insulated by their smugness and protected by their own appointed army of executive and special assistants from the economic problems facing Canadians. It was these economic problems that brought mass violence and riots to the city of Montreal, and these economic problems which brought us a summer of strikes in our major mining and industrial complexes, strikes which have continued into the fall. All the while, the vast numbers of self-employed Canadians have suffered grimly, and quietly tried to carry on, but at the same time wondering: "How long, O Lord, how long will my tax burdens keep increasing?"
We find the following words in the throne speech:
There are many obstacles to be overcome if we are to achieve our economic goals, but inflation is undoubtedly the most serious and the most difficult to control. If we fail to control it, the consequences could rapidly prove disastrous especially, but not only, for those whose incomes are already low.
Why did you not do something about inflation while there was still time? I remind the Liberal government that they have been in power since 1963 and the Governor of the Bank of Canada, in each of his annual reviews, warned them each year that inflation must be stopped. However, each year the response was the same and the warnings have been ignored. In 1963, following the election, it was a Liberal program called "60 days of decision" which aided inflation, followed a little later by a program entitled "let us get

The Address-Mr. Crouse the economy rolling again" while the economic signs at that time indicated that what the government should have been doing was putting on the brakes. But there was an election to be won in 1965, so the Liberal attitude seemed to be not to worry about the state of the economy. Following their return to office, we soon learned about the new method of ending strikes which was called "the Pearson formula or 30 per cent". This formula was unnecessary and inflationary and it set the pattern for all future demands.
When our currency was devalued in 1962 to 92.5 per cent in relation to the U.S. dollar, in an effort to stimulate and increase our exports, it was to be a temporary measure. This move brought considerable economic benefits to Canada but the Liberal government of the day dissipated the advantages through government extravagance, and the present government is still doing this. Again, these are not only my views.
