Thank you, Mr. Speaker. These are not my views alone. They are endorsed again in today's Financial Times in the following words:
There can be no doubt about the contribution of former government wastefulness to the present inflationary problem. The rolling of the money presses caused by government over-spending was central in getting the economy into the mess it is in now.
The strains which the free-spending policies of the past created should be sufficient proof that governments at all levels can no longer afford to waste a penny...
...the past few years have shown that, if the economy is to be kept under control, governments must choose their priorities with the knowledge that there is a strict ceiling on the amounts they can spend.
The trouble with this government is that they say one thing while they do another.
Let me return to the throne speech, and to the following words in it:
In recent months the government has urged both the public and the private sectors to adopt special measures to combat the dangers of inflation. These measures, which the government has itself adopted, must be applied by all if further restraints are to be avoided.
What hypocrisy and what arrogance! The government asks the public to follow its example, but I say: heaven forbid, or we will be in national bankruptcy and West Germany or the United States, which have the strongest currencies, will buy up this country.



University in Nova Scotia and from Memorial University in St. John's, Newfoundland. The subsidy for the construction of wooden ships has been removed, resulting in some shipyards closing down while others have reduced their work force by 90 per cent in the last two years. You have taken away the inshore sealing rights.
This action of cutting down the subsidy for wooden ships has stopped the modernization of the wooden fishing fleet. If this course is continued, the present fleet could become obsolete within a few years. How can you justify paying a 35 per cent subsidy on a steel hull without paying the same amount for a wooden hull? Is this the just society as applied to our wooden shipbuilders? The 35 per cent subsidy should be paid on wooden ships as well as steel, since the fishing equipment installed in these ships is identical.
Having removed practically all the fishermen's bandaids, what are you planning to offer them in return? Surely, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when he was studying for his black belt-I am sorry he is not in his seat- learned that if you wish to push someone forward you first act as if you wish to push him backward. This brings opposing forces into play on your behalf making the push forward a simple matter. Surely, our fishermen have been pushed backward far enough and the time is ripe to offer them some incentives to go forward. The record will show that the market value of the fish landed in Nova Scotia this year exceeds $100 million and it is reasonable to assume that at least 10 per cent of this amount will find its way back into the tax coffers of the nation in one way or another. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that 70 per cent of this money is new wealth, as that is the percentage of the catch exported to the United States. This amount must certainly help to meet the balance of payments on imports. I would therefore suggest that you give some of the money that you are taking from the fishing industry back to that industry.
In my native province $1 million a year in subsidy funds for wooden ships would enable Nova Scotia to maintain a fleet competitive with the highly subsidized fleets of other countries operating in the Grand Banks area. However, if you plan to cut out subsidies altogether, we will watch with interest to see if this same policy applies to the CBC and the National Arts Centre. Surely, if our productive industries must stand or fall on their
The Address-Mr. Crouse own efforts, the same rule of thumb must apply to entertainment fields. Having provided a $47 million Arts Centre for our national arts there would really be no justification for an annual subsidy toward entertainment in excess of $2J million, which I notice is the amount listed in the estimates for 1969-70.
Since our fishermen will need new ships, I would suggest that the government provide an incentive for their construction by permitting the cost of any new ship to be written off as an investment allowance, without payment of taxes on earnings, over a three-year period. I would point out also that any nation that has cut out assistance to the fishing industry, such as the United States and Sweden, has noted a decline in the over-all catch landed by that industry.
Since the men engaged in the fishing industry are exposed to many hardships-and young men today are not training to become fishermen-I suggest that they be placed in a special category for income tax purposes. This could take one of two forms. At present, if a citizen is over 70 years of age, he may claim a $500 age exemption on payment of his income tax. I suggest that fishermen should also be permitted this exemption. Alternatively, in view of the fact that their fishing operations are depleting our fishing resources, a fact which has been brought to our attention by scientists, a fisherman's income should be treated in the same manner as taxable income from some Canadian corporations for which a 15 to 20 per cent depletion allowance is accep'able to the government. I believe this special recognition would encourage more men to become fishermen. It would constitute a recognition of the hazards and uncertainties associated with the occupation, while assisting in the future growth and expansion of this important east coast industry.
Speaking as a member of parliament from Atlantic Canada, I believe that improvement in the transportation links between our area and central Canada could go a long way toward solving problems of regional disparity. We had hoped, through area incentives, that Atlantic Canada would have something extra to offer when seeking new industries, but this cabinet has changed all that. This same provision has been extended to a wide area of Canadian territory, taking away our special advantages and enabling the richer provinces to further widen the economic gap between us. However, maritimers are immune to adversity by now and almost numb from the
Oclober 27, 1969

The Address-Mr. Benjamin beating given us by some of your programs. However, we still keep fighting, we still keep trying.
Since our railroad system is not the shortest route to Montreal, and we have not had any serious disagreements with the Americans in recent years, I should like to propose that the present government take a real step forward by advocating to the government of the United States a joint construction program on a corridor road through Maine. This road, linking the trans-Canada highway of the maritimes with Sherbrooke and Montreal, would cover some 180 miles of American territory but it would shorten the route between our area and central Canada and enable us to deliver our products more quickly. I realize the responsibility for constructing this road would rest solely with the United States but surely, with the new oil finds on the northern slopes in Alaska and the need for the rights-of-way for pipe lines through Canadian territory, some suitable agreement could be reached between our government and the government of the United States. In this way the needs and aspirations of our citizens could be met and we would be able to ensure the "progress and greatness of Canada", in the words of the Speech from the Throne. In Atlantic Canada we are still waiting for some sign of the Prime Minister's just society. In my view, a new transportation link between Atlantic Canada and the vast markets in central Canada would go a long way toward making the just society a reality in our area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before embarking on the main part of my comments I am tempted, and will yield to the temptation, to comment upon some of the matters raised in the Speech from the Throne. First, I was struck by the lack of attention in the speech to the critical problem of Canadian economic independence. It seems to me that only when the Government of Canada, and the nation as a whole, have greater control of the ownership of this economy will we be able to really do a job of directing our economy and controlling inflation. To my mind, the casual reference in the speech to farm marketing and income is most outrageous and I shall have more to say about that later. The much talked of Canada Development Corporation, which previous Liberal governments put forward, however weak and anemic it might have been, has again been

shelved. The Liberals either are not concerned about this- or are so completely enmeshed in the webb of outside corporations which own an ever increasing share of Canada that this government has been frozen into inaction.
The speech also forecasts extensive reform of our taxation system. We shall have to see what this entails. I suggest that the main needs are these: We must have a better redistribution of the tax load, a capital gains tax, a tightening of depreciation and incentive allowances for the mining and resource industries and the provision of higher exemptions and increased tax allowances for families with children. The speech also mentioned that the voting age in this country will be lowered. Mr. Speaker, in Saskatchewan we did that 25 years ago; our response to this measure therefore is automatic. As in so many other things, this Liberal government is 25 years behind the times.
On the matter of housing the speech seems to indicate that the government plans for the future more of what we have had in the past. If that assumption is right, then the Liberals again have missed the point. What we need is not just more houses, but houses at prices which more people can afford, with mortgages carrying interest rates which any of us can afford. Also, on the subject of inflation, unless moves to control inflation include more vigorous action with respect to the corporate sector of our economy, the results of action taken will continue to be disappointing. I suggest two moves the government can make. I suggest the control of profits through taxation, and greater influence by government on how corporations spend and re-invest profits accumulated in Canada. I shall have more to say about that in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker.
While the fight against inflation has been mentioned, we have heard about this government's expenditures on ministerial offices. Reference has been made to the Prime Minister's staff and to the renovation of ministers' offices. There are to be larger ministerial staffs and all kinds of expenses are to be undertaken which show that this government is as arrogant as other Liberal governments have been. Something that was drawn to my attention a few weeks ago illustrates how arrogant this government is. You know, Mr. Speaker, many great things, some of them quite justifiable, have been said about the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). It now appears that his worth can be measured. His
October 27, 1969	COMMONS
worth is equal to four ounces and $6.50. Why do I say that? On September 22 the minister made a speech to the annual convention of the Canadian Airline Employees' Association. On Thursday, September 25 the text of the speech arrived at the editorial office of the Regina Leader Post. The speech weighed four ounces and had cost $6.50 to send by air express. I should like to know if the Minister of Labour makes a practice of sending copies of his speeches to all newspapers and radio and television stations in Canada? I should like to know that, because I do not think the action taken was proper. I do not suppose the minister sent the speech, but I should like to know what idiot in his office authorized $6.50 of the taxpayer's money to be spent on sending a four ounce speech by air express.
As I said, I was shocked to see that the Speech from the Throne made such casual reference to problems of farm marketing and income. Two paragraphs in the speech referred to the subject. Finally, after being prodded for many months, the government has made an admission. The Speech from the Throne reads in part as follows:
One of Canada's most valuable assets is undeniably the richness and variety of her material resources. In some cases, production has increased substantially and outstripped demand; grain is one of the commodities of which reserves have piled up,-
Everybody else in Canada knows that, and now the government has admitted it.
In the throne speech the government indicates that it will amend the Canada Grain Act. In my opinion this action is long overdue since very likely it will improve our position on world markets. Yet there is not one word in the speech about strengthening and enlarging the Canadian Wheat Board, and there is not one proposal about farm incomes and the marketing of farm products.
The throne speech also mentions the agricultural crisis through which we are going. We already know that. My party, members of the official opposition and of the Creditiste group, have advanced many proposals during the last year; farm organizations have come up with all kinds of specific proposals, yet the government has not chosen to act on any of them. Few members of the government seemed to listen to proposals made about farm incomes in western Canada. Members of the official opposition recommended a system of acreage payments, as did spokesmen for farm organizations. Our party
DEBATES	117
The Address-Mr. Benjamin recommended the implementation of deficiency payments, as did members of farm organizations. Almost all in this house were unanimous in recommending a two-price system for wheat in conjunction with these payments, yet the government took no action. The government has not said why the adoption of the recommended course of action would not be appropriate.
In my opinion, the government's policy, as outlined in the Speech from the Throne, will be to take advantage of the farm crisis, to cause further tens of thousands of farmers to be eliminated from the agricultural industry. That suits the government's purposes. It suits the government not to help farmers with their cash income problem because it wants to speed up the process under which the number of farms is reduced. A small further reduction in the number of people farming is probably inevitable; but surely this process can be carried out over a long term and in a more civilized and humane manner. Too many viable, economic farm units will fall victims to the grand design of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the government of Canada which seeks to eliminate more farms from the agricultural industry. The government has not as yet properly researched the social and financial loss accruing to the entire community as a result of the further drastic reduction in farm population. I submit that this cost to the community far exceeds any cost that might be involved in maintaining the present number of people on farm units.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I wish to say a few words about the Canadian Wheat Board. I congratulate the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) for Sas-katoon-Humboldt on his appointment. I was under the impression that he held his present job last year. He acted, I thought, in his present capacity in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) who was ill and who has now returned to work. In any event, I congratulate him. The conditions under which the Canadian Wheat Board can operate are the same as they were one year ago. We still face the mess we faced one year ago with respect to the need for box cars, the fair allocation of cars and the delivery of grain to the elevator of the farmer's choice. May I say in reference to the allocation of railway equipment that the DBS figure for carloadings of wheat and other grains on western lines in an 11 week period


The Address-Mr. Benjamin from August 1, the beginning of the crop year, to the 14th of this October shows that some 2,700 fewer cars were loaded in this period compared to a year ago and almost
7,000	fewer than loaded in the same period in 1967.
A week ago, Mr. Speaker, I met with representatives from the eight wheat pool committees in rural Saskatchewan. Each of them submitted reports to me on the situation in their particular area. Each of them confirmed that they are in a worse position than they were a year ago. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) also met with some wheat pool committees in an area close to that which I represent. I am certain he can report receiving the same kind of information from those committees.
The reports were unanimous in pointing out these areas were still on the unit quota and had not yet delivered 400 bushels per farmer. Some still had not delivered the extra one bushel they are entitled to deliver as a result of their inability to complete the five bushel quota a year ago. All of them reported the desperate financial position of every farmer. All of them felt that cash advances were just another loan that partially postponed the problem and made the day of reckoning all the more horrible to contemplate.
I am going to put on the record a policy statement adopted by my party in the province of Saskatchewan. I am immodest enough to claim some part in the authorship of this statement because there have been speeches made by other spokesmen, from both the federal and provincial Liberal governments in Saskatchewan, laying blame on the Canadian Wheat Board for the position we are in regarding our export markets. I would like to submit that the blame for the situation the western farmer is in rests solely and completely upon the federal Liberal government, aided and abetted by their counterparts in Saskatchewan. Their attempts to shift blame on to the Canadian Wheat Board must not be allowed to succeed.
The Wheat Board can only operate within the limits of federal government policy. The policies of the present government have served to effectively handcuff the Board and prevent it from doing the best possible job for western farmers. These policies also serve to perpetuate the operations of the private grain trade, at the expense of western farmers, and at the same time to undermine the principle of orderly marketing through a central public agency.

For example, the fact that the Wheat Board must deal through foreign, privately owned grain traders cannot be in the best interests of western farmers or the Canadian nation as a whole and serves as a stricture on Canadian sales in world markets. The turning of a blind eye to provincial and interprovincial trafficking in grain at firesale prices is further evidence of the Liberal government's failure to act in the interests of farmers.
My party, Mr. Speaker, reaffirms its support for the Canadian Wheat Board. Our provincial council calls for an even further enlarging of the responsibilities and activities of the Board, backed by the government of the whole nation. If Liberal governments really do believe in, and support, the Canadian Wheat Board, and the principle of orderly marketing through a public agency, it is time they put their action where their mouth is.
We call on the government to act immediately to, one; bring flax, rye, rapeseed and feed grains under the complete jurisdiction of the Board; two, authorize and pay for the expansion of the facilities and operation of the Board into market and product research, sales offices and staff in importing countries; three, empower the Board to have complete control and direction of grain handling including all transportation facilities needed for the grain movement.
The mess in the railway industry in particular, that part designated to handle our grain and grain products, is as bad as ever and still continues after many years. We have previously suggested the appointment of a controller. This did not seem to suit the government. We now suggest the entire responsibility and authority necessary for the movement of railway equipment for the transportation of grain be placed in the hands of, and under the direction of, the Canadian Wheat Board. As a fourth point, we urge that the government authorize the Board to establish its own grain brokerage agency in order to bypass domestic and foreign private grain trade speculators and, fifth, embody in Wheat Board legislation the principle of the right of farmers to deliver their grain to the elevator of their choice.
This principle has been expounded and pleaded for by political parties, farm organizations and individual farmers since the days of the Bracken Commission-perhaps even before that. There have been some attempts, on paper or in theory, to implement it. When one sees shipping point after shipping point
Ociober 27, 1969

at which the farmers' own elevator companies are outrageously discriminated against in the allocation of railway equipment, resulting in the percentage of their market dropping from 65 and 75 per cent to 40 and 45 per cent, one finds an indication this government is more interested in the survival of the private grain trade which has been a parasite on the back of western farmers since Canada began.
A sixth point we would like to make is that there should be provision for added farmer representation on the Board. In addition to these six points I have mentioned, and there are many more I could go into which would strengthen and widen the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board, there is a further measure I think many people in this country feel the government should take. We call on the government to institute a system of guaranteed prices based on costs of production and at the same time give the Canadian Wheat Board the freedom to sell in the export market at the most advantageous prices. Whenever those export prices are below the guaranteed price, the national treasury should make up the difference.
Reference was made last Friday by the leader of my party, and by the two previous speakers, to inflation, the steel industry and steel prices. I would like now to dwell a bit on this point if I may. The government's concern for inflation is somewhat justified. All of us must have some concern for it, but when that concern develops into a pre-occupation that goes to the lengths of perpetrating hardships on hundreds of thousands of Canadians while privileged corporations and individuals go merrily on their way, then this or any other government is guilty of the grossest of governmental malpractice.
This government, in the classic old line party so-called free enterprise style, is waging war on inflation by attacking the very people who have in no way contributed to inflation and in fact are the first victims of it. This government forgot about the old age pensioner, old age assistance recipients, veterans on pension, retired R.C.M.P., civil service pensioners, fishermen, unorganized workers and small businessmen. Surely, these are not the people who caused or who are contributing to inflation. Surely, the government's failure to act in their interest is a backwards attack on inflation. The government, in its cutbacks, is hurting its own employees and striking at sections of the economy which are already depressed. According to the DBS summary of

The Address-Mr. Benjamin interest-the country and the public interest be damned.
Apologists for the steel industry, who include some hon. members in the old parties on both sides of this House, will frantically point a finger at wage increases as justification for the increase in steel prices. As has been the case on previous occasions it is certain that most of the cost of wage increases, and, probably, all of the cost, will be more than offset by increases in productivity. When the final figures are published I bet the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs a new bat that this will prove to be is the case. Let me quote from a letter addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) by Mr. William Mahoney, the Canadian director of the United Steelworkers union. This letter is dated October 22. It deals with this question of steel price increases, and states, in part:
We want to make It very clear that, in the opinion of the United Steelworkers of America, the settlement terms just approved by our members do not justify any increase in prices. The wage increases and benefit improvements outlined in that settlement can be completely met out of the improvement in productivity achieved by our members over the period of the previous collective agreement.
Government and industry figures on the productivity of our members employed by the basic steel industry were recently analyzed by our union. We sent the details to you, to members of your government, to members of the House and to editors of all major Canadian publications well in advance of this year's negotiations. Figures for the first six months of this year which were not available at that time, confirm that our members' productivity has continued to grow.
We want to emphasize that despite the fact that our members earned their wage increases and benefit improvements in advance it was still necessary for them to go through negotiations, government conciliation, government mediation and finally, go without pay for over eighty days before they could secure those wage increases and benefit improvements. Furthermore, unlike the steel industry, our members will not get special tax treatment, enabling them to use their income loss this year to offset higher earnings in other years.
The letter goes on:
In contrast, the steel industry can simply announce price increases after a unilateral management decision.
This is a dramatic example of the basic imbalance between government treatment of wage income and government treatment of investor income in Canada. This is the imbalance which must be corrected before your recently-appointed Prices and Incomes Commission can be accepted in good faith by Canadian workers. This is also a dramatic opportunity for your government to correct the imbalance.

We suggest that your government ask the industry to withhold any increase in steel prices until such time as the steel companies can justify such price increases to their customers and to the general public before an appropriate government-appointed Board of Enquiry or the Prices and Incomes Commission itself.
This letter underlines more forcibly than I can, the need for these corporations, particularly those associated with basic industry, to justify the price increases they place on their products. Incidentally, this time I have not heard the steel industry using the old chestnut that wage increases have brought about these increases in price. The only justification the industry has put forward so far, to my knowledge, is that many of the products to which these increases apply have not been increased in price for two and a half years.
Upon examination, this becomes the most spurious excuse of all. There sure as hell was no justification for an increase during the last two and a half years. If one looks at the profits made by tiie Steel Company of Canada one finds that in 1964 they amounted to $43,630,000, in 1965 to $45,454,000 and in 1966 to $42,774,000. Now, we come to the period in which the industry says it did not raise its prices. In 1967 the profits were $46,733,000 and in 1968 they were no less than $67,971,000. By the way, these are profits after taxation-net profits. I maintain that having made a profit in 1968 amounting to almost $68 million the government and the country could more properly have expected a price decrease of 6 per cent rather than an increase; the Steel Company of Canada would still be doing extremely well. The ratio of net profit to shareholder's equity in this company was 10.5 per cent in 1967. This was not bad, you will say. Well, in 1968 it had risen to 14.1 per cent. How's that for a fat return? Surely, it is more than can be considered fair and reasonable by comparison with what the big majority of Canadians received as a result of salary and pension increases. And, as we know, farm income actually dropped.
I would point out that corporations such as the Steel Company of Canada are virtually immune to inflationary pressures; they are little affected by tight money and high interest rates. From their large reserves of retained profits they can easily lend themselves the necessary money for plant improvement and expansion at zero per cent. They are also-obviously-not obliged to respond to anti-inflationary measures which the government calls upon itself or upon the


private sector to take. The tragedy is that the multiplier effect of an increase in steel prices, as the products pass through the hands of the manufacturer, the wholesaler and the retailer, will mean that the consumer must pay many times more than the 6 per cent increase I have mentioned. The increase in the basic price will provide a neat cover for automobile, truck and farm machinery manufacturers, enabling them to add an even greater increase to the price of their products, since it opens a beautiful opportunity to make bigger and better profits which can all be blamed on higher steel prices. At the end of the line is the victimized consumer and the private enterprise government which has egg on its face for allowing aid and comfort to privileged friends. Meanwhile, inflation rolls merrily along.
Surely, this is one area in which the government should require restraint. Surely, the government ought now to force a roll-back of an unjustifiable steel price increase. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read with great attention the traditional Speech from the Throne which depicts existing conditions and sets in uncertain terms the government's attitude towards the present economic situation.
A rather lengthy list of new bills has also been tabled and I presume that more details can be expected during this session concerning what the government intends to do about measures taken to reduce unemployment, that social ailment whose ravages must be restricted by every means at our disposal.
In agriculture, the government will have to define its position in order to boost the morale of farmers who are still faced with nearly insoluble problems which will force a great many of them to sell their land or declare bankruptcy.
Many other problems will require definite legislation and I wish that we may be able during this session to pass practical legislative measures in the interest of the population which expects from the government more comprehension and action than useless debate.
I have listened with interest to those who have participated in the debate until now. The mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne have performed very well considering the circumstances. The representatives of the various


The Address-Mr. Dionne parties all deserve congratulations. I do not doubt that each one of them has expounded his point of view according to his convictions.
I hope it will be recognized that many problems could find a solution if everyone made an effort to understand the ideas expressed by the members of the various parties and to ascertain as wisely as possible to what extent each one really works for the welfare of the country, rather than to promote the interests of one's own party.
In this century of materialism, it is too often forgotten that ideas are at the root of any improvement, however small.
The author of the best editorial for 1968, according to the Canadian Association of French Weeklies, which comprises 107 newspapers, simply headlined his article with these two words: "Good Idea."
He was speaking with much common sense, and I would like to quote parts of that article:
Ideas are as invisible and airy as electricity. Yet, it has been possible to pick up the electric fluid with wires and aerials. Why should it not be possible to pick up the "intellectual fluid" by more sophisticated means like silence, study and meditation. Let us open our mind still more to new ideas. Let us find them in the jumble oi thoughts that beset our mind at every moment.
He ends his article on these words:
Do not tell me that an idea is worthless. There is something good in every idea; there are only men not willing to take advantage of ideas. Any idea as a whole can bring forth a better one. The needle was invented before the sewing machine. Any idea is the road to a sure development.
I hope the ideas expressed during this session will not be misconstrued nor wrongly implemented, in order to lead to a better understanding of the causes of the difficulties experienced by Canadians. We must also wish that we will find through the exchange of good ideas practical solutions to the numerous economic problems of today.
If we consider long enough the principle that production is aimed at consumption, we shall realize easily that the purpose of production is not reached, and we shall be more prepared to look for the causes of this in the distribution system.
Several economists contend that amortization is now part of the purchasing power. However, it is very difficult to assess its lag and to determine its influence and scope on the immediate availability in terms of purchasing power in the hands of consumers. One or two factors of this kind are enough to reverse the position of recognized experts.

Besides, daily evidence shows us that the purchasing power available to consumers is undoubtedly inadequate.
I have before me an article published in Le Devoir in October 1962, following a television broadcast of October 4 during which two different theories had been explained by members of parliament on the problem of wealth distribution. Mr. P. H. Lavallee, an engineer, called the readers' attention to an idea originating with Major C. H. Douglas, also an engineer and the founder of Social Credit, who explored this field through differential calculus (in which time is considered as an operator. One may well wonder whether his position is not closer to reality.
Mr. Lavallee stated, and I quote:
Where experimental science is concerned, when a system cannot be based on facts, one uses an hypothesis. On the latter one builds a theory which must bring one to the solution one is seeking.
For example, Copernicus Galileo assumed that the earth could rotate around the sun, as the result of which many astronomical problems were solved. Christopher Columbus assumed that the earth was round, and we know what happened. On the other hand, Pasteur went on from the hypothesis (current then) of the infinitesimal. Modern atomic science is based wholly on a hypothesis-that of the structure of the atom. When a hypothesis is inconsistent with the facts, only once, it is rejected and a new one is used.
As for the problem which interests us at the present time, it is fair to proceed in the same way.
Let us state a first hypothesis: The purchasing power provided by production is sufficient to dispose of the latter. How can we explain then that in a normal period, we are often faced with overproduction or rather acute sub-consumption? Great numbers of people would like, in vain, to buy the goods which pack warehouses. There is also unemployment. In short, we are faced with the problem of abundance.
How can we explain that this uneasiness diminishes or disappears in wartime or when the economy is in full progress or, even, when the trade balance of a country is favourable?
Second hypothesis: Production alone cannot finance consumption. If we still want to balance our economy, we must make up for a shortage of purchasing lower. The supplement could take different forms.
Having said what happens in wartime:
(1)	With regard to the wages of soldiers and workers employed in war factories (unsold production which cannot be bought);

(2)	Massive capitalization for important projects;
(3)	Favourable trade balance. Realizing that the last two methods are not sufficient to fill the gap between prices and buying power, Mr. Lavallee adds that another method must be used, and I quote:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The distribution of additional purchasing power to the citizens of the country so as to sell the whole production.
It is always argued that this measure will lead to inflation as if there was no middle term nor any middle course between a chronic shortage of purchasing power and inflation.
If the issue of additional funds is strictly and scientifically controlled, there should not be more inflation than when the Aluminum Company took the decision to invest several hundred million dollars at Kitimat or when the Iron Ore and Quebec Cartier Mining decided to sink more than half a million dollars in Labrador; nor when the St. Lawrence Seaway or the Dew line were built; no more than when it was decided to pay family allowances or old age pensions. But it might be possible to find there a means to balance and stabilize the economy.
Considering the remarks I have just made, the classic economists' position does not seem to me to be unassailable, and I am wondering if the second hypothesis has not at least as many chances to be valid as the first one.
It seemed desirable to me to submit this idea at the beginning of the session and I think I have used wisely the time allotted to me, by promoting the concept of the distribution of abundance rather than praise the government on its achievements or criticize it for what it failed to do.
I shall undoubtedly have an opportunity to take part in the debates on some of the bills we will have to consider during this session. However, I am convinced that if we could direct the legislative work towards this idea of a more equitable distribution of goods, most Canadians would be satisfied with the administration of their country and would be better prepared to respect the government's authority that needs to be strengthened.
Before closing, I should like to say that the Speech from the Throne mentions the government's resolve to achieve linguistic equality. The Official Languages Act constitutes a pressing invitation to all the provinces to take that course which will help save Canadian unity.	.	.

There is no provision in the act which compels Canadians to speak English and French. But it recognizes existing facts. This gesture has an important symbolic value which should help bring about true bilingualism at the federal level.
Canada is a federation of ten provinces and constitutes a country. In matters of general interest we must act as Canadians and not only as residents of a province.
English is known throughout the world as the commercial language and French as the diplomatic one. Therefore, there is some advantage in having both official languages on an equal footing in Canada and in having them in use in all parts of the country where conditions permit.
The development of interprovincial co-operation could become easier and greatly help to achieve the desired goal; makes a new Canada that will recognize in fact the equality of the two founding peoples.
I would urge all those who are not yet won over to read a speech given by Mr. Douglas How, editor in chief of the Reader's Digest, on October 16, 1963, at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel, about "The Canadians that we could be".
On the first page Mr. How states, and I quote:
What French Canada is asking for would, in a large measure, correspond to what we, Englishspeaking Canadians, consider necessary in Canada.
And later on he adds:
Through and in spite of this resistance we have created the Canada of today. In making its inventory, English Canada would do well to remember that the miracle of the survival of French Canada played a leading part in the survival of Canada as an independent state.
On the other hand, it would not be a bad thing for French Canada to remember that such a miracle was only possible on account of English Canada. We needed one another. What remains to be seen is whether we can convince one another to maintain that kind of co-operation.
Otherwise, should this country break up, we will have to conclude that we were not strong enough to make the best of our opportunities and to take up the challenges inherent in them. Therefore the tragedy then would not consist in such a division, which would be but the logical result of a matter of fact. The tragedy would consist in not having been able to become what we could have been. Such is the essence of our history, of the present crisis, of our future. We can overcome such a difficulty and add to our size. But if we do not overcome it, we run the risk of losing ground-and even worse.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of representing the people of the Winnipeg South Centre constituency, in this parliament of which so much is expected. To me, it is a great honour as well as a great task.

As we come into our one hundredth year in Manitoba, which is a province that has featured both languages so strongly in its history, I think it is only fitting that I should try, in my own small way to accept that fact by struggling slightly to begin my speech in French.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

Why not continue in French?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
I would love to be able to do so. I guarantee that six or seven years from now I shall be able to do so.
Some hon. members may have noticed on the front of my car a distinctive looking licence plate bearing the number 100 and saying "Manitoba-The First 'In' Province". This is a sort of gimmick adopted by the province of Manitoba this year to draw attention to the fact that on July 15, 1970 we will be celebrating the hundredth anniversary of our entry into confederation. Although we were not a party to the original negotiations which resulted in the Dominion of Canada, we joined the dominion three years and 15 days after it had been born. So, we were the first "in" province, as my licence plate declares to all and sundry, and we are very proud of it.
It was in Manitoba that the separate thrusts of English and French penetration of this continent collided, and in Winnipeg, where the Red and Assiniboine rivers meet, where these two peoples resolved, after an initial clash, to bed down together and, with the native Indians of the area, build a distinctive little colony of their own. It was here that the good faith of the new Canadian confederation was first put to the test.
As the centennial of Manitoba draws near, the name of Louis Riel looms large in my home town. Like myself, he was a member of

parliament. He was elected to this House three times but he was never allowed to take his seat. Yet, he retains a claim to a place in history, for it was he who insisted that the colony of Assiniboia must only join Canada on negotiated terms acceptable to the people who lived in it. He was not a French Canadian; he was a French speaking citizen of the Northwest. Just as W. L. McKenzie and Joseph Papineau had insisted some 30 years before in Ontario and Quebec, he insisted on representation by population for the west.
Probably Riel should be considered Manitoba's Father of Confederation. He was not its sole founder-I do not think it is right to call him the founder of Manitoba as some people want to do today-although assuredly he was one of the founders. Others would include Chief Henry Prince, who signed the first treaty between Canada and the Indians of the Northwest

it was treaty number one signed in 1871-and who spoke for his people as their elected delegate in the troubles of 1869 and 1870 in which Riel first featured. He was descended from Chief Peguis, who in turn negotiated and signed the original treaty with Lord Selkirk in 1819.
The Earl of Selkirk was another person whom we should consider as another founder of Manitoba. He established the first permanent settlement in the Northwest by bringing Irish and Scottish dispossessed crofters to this land and setting them up on the banks of the river.
Then, there was Alexander K. Isbister, a native of the Red River region, a man of mixed blood, who headed a delegation to the British government in 1846. His- efforts resulted ultimately in some measure of local representation on the Hudson Bay Company's governing board.
Then, we have Louis Riel senior, the father of the man who was more famous, who helped to establish free trade and break the Hudson Bay Company's monopoly in the entire Northwest.
Then, we have a Nova Scotian, Adams George Archibald, the first Manitoba lieutenant governor. By his insistence on "keeping his cool" on all questions and by his determined fairness to all factions he guided Manitoba through its first difficult years and set the pattern for tolerance and justice of which we are all so rightly proud. After Archibald there were many others, many natural leaders who emerged from the countless immigrants who flooded into our land


and made it what it is today. So, I suggest that Riel is our Father of Confederation, and many more people share my view regarding his claim to be founder of Manitoba.
What has all this to do with us here and now? I suggest that if we want to know where we are going, we must sometimes pause to look backwards to see where we have been. It is useful also to note that although Manitoba's boundaries have expanded greatly since it came to confederation as the postage stamp province, and its population now exceeds one million people, we still consider ourselves to be a region, or part of a region, distinct and unique from all the others.
Confederation is attractive to us now, as the idea of Canada was attractive one hundred years ago, only to the degree that it allows us to contribute in our own way to Canada as a whole. We came in voluntarily one hundred years ago and we remain in the confederation voluntarily as the beginning of our second century looms ahead; but now, as then, we have our own distinctive ideas about how some of Canada's remaining problems should be solved.
In the Speech from the Throne I noted many subjects of interest to us all. We are all interested in the reform of the United Nations; we are all interested in the idea of a Canadian international development research centre; we are all interested in helping our Indian and Eskimo peoples to help themselves; we are all interested in the subjects of social security, amendments to collective bargaining laws, the enforcement of measures to fight inflation, the fight against pollution, further amendments to the Criminal Code, consumer protection laws, etc.
But there are some items that to me will test the government's seriousness of intent in so far as regional equality is concerned. I commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for his continued efforts to revise our constitution and for his statement that the federal constitution must always provide for the integrity of the regions or provinces making up the state. I am intrigued by his suggestion that the four Senate divisions of Canada might be used as the basis for developing a consensus on certain matters. In this connection, it is interesting to note that Sir Alexander T. Galt, one of the more able Fathers of Confederation, wanted a Senate in which some approach to federal equality between the various sections of the country would be 21362-9
The Address-Mr. Osier secured, and felt very firmly that we should have an upper house elected on a territorial basis to give some weight to the legitimate differences of opinion between regions which would otherwise be swamped in a legislative assembly elected on the basis of population.
It is good to see that the federal government proposes to increase funds to reduce regional disparities, and it will be interesting indeed to discover whether the white paper on taxation aimed at achieving a fairer distribution of the tax burden has any features in it that might provide a sort of built-in compensation for those of us who live in parts of the country that appear to offer less glamorous opportunities than the central provinces. It is gratifying to see that we will have amendments to the Canada Grains Act. While no one can hope to sell a commodity such as grain as easily as it used to be sold in the good old days, it is only common sense to bring our system of grading and marketing into line with the systems that prevail among our competitors.
In housing, and particularly in urban renewal, I hope to see some formula adopted that is not a simple freeze. Just as the government intends to emphasize measures to help low income families in housing, I hope they will consider measures to help in a special way low income regions to catch up with the more affluent parts of this country.
This is not a land where all can be centralized; it is too vast, too complex and too diverse for that. The glory of Canada will be found in the quality of the lives of the people living in all sorts of places, in all sorts of styles. We are not enamoured of the melting pot theory, thank God. We should rejoice as much in the achievement of Didi Woolgar, who runs an art shop of quality on the ground floor of a Yellowknife hotel, as we do about the National Arts Centre across from Parliament Hill. Perhaps we should rejoice more over Didi's achievement, and others like her, than over the ones that are so finished and final.
My fellow members from Winnipeg-of whom I see one across the House right now- will no doubt remember, as I do, the seeds that have grown into our own magnificent centennial hall and the cultural achievements of Winnipeg. When I was a boy the people of Winnipeg heard concerts in the old Grace Church and the old Board of Trade building, where the performers had to compete with the noise from shunting engines in the Canadian National yards nearby. What was


The Address-Mr. McIntosh developed in these unlikely places was art indigenous to the skills of our own peoples, so that what we have today in Winnipeg is founded firmly and is not imposed upon our people from on high. This is as it should be because the exciting truth is we are a "becoming" nation and we must build for ourselves as we go along, and seek our own solutions.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
We hear a lot about the search for a Canadian identity. Professional panelists make their livings searching vainly for this elusive thing before the beady eyes of television cameras-in colour, yet! They search in vain, for the thing they look for is already there, had they only the wit to see it.
Not long ago I attended the marriage of two young friends of mine. The bridegroom's heritage was Scots-in-Canada for 170 years, plus French-in-Canada for 300; the bride's people had been living in Canada since long before the middle of the nineteenth century. Why search for an identity here? Why look for things that all 20 million of us should now be taking for granted, and working as hard as we know how to improve?
There are some among us who dissent loudly and clearly about many things they think are wrong with this country today. Thank God they have the right to do so, so long as they respect the rights of others in the process. Things can be improved ;they ought to be improved; they must be improved. But as we go about this process of improving the quality of life in Canada today let us remember the monument to Jacques Cartier on Gaspe's rugged coast, and also the memorial to the bush pilots of Canada that stands on the summit of a harsh peninsula jutting out into Great Slave Lake beside one of the most isolated capital cities in the world. For more than 400 years men have been striving to make of this a great country. We must continue to do the same.

speechtext:
Unfortunately, Mr. Minister, it fails to inform us how this concern will be translated into action. There was passing reference, too, to the bogey of inflation. But again any suggestion of action on the part of the government was exceedingly vague. All in all, the speech was most notable for what it did not say, for the areas that were untouched, for the problems by-passed or ignored. Whether this was intentional or not, we are not at this time prepared to say.
I have in mind one particular group of Canadians who, apparently, were entirely overlooked. This is the large number of solid Canadian citizens forced to subsist on fixed incomes. Forgetting them is crime enough, but to emphasize their chief enemy, inflation, without giving any hope of remedial action, is unforgiveable.
Pensioners, particularly retired federal public servants, are a ghost army that must haunt any government with a conscience, but one which the present government has obviously deliberately excluded from the fabric of the so-called just socie'y. I believe they constitute a spectre that will torment the government in the months ahead.
These retired persons do not enjoy the general benefits that flow from rising incomes and improved living standards. They are the helpless targets of inflation. With fixed incomes and diminishing purchasing power, they suffer most. Some of them have some measure of flexibility, through personal initiative, to try to off-set the ravages of inflation. Others are dependent upon pension plans or superannuation schemes, provincial or private, that are more modern, more effective and more humane than is the federal system. It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that I wish to confine what I have to say to the plight of the superannuated public servants of Canada.
For a long time now, through their chosen bargaining agents, public servants have sought to have superannuation included as a
October 27, 1969	COMMONS
bargainable point during collective bargaining sessions. They have described the present system as inadequate and antiquated and feel, rightly I believe, that they should be allowed to contribute their ideas to modernizing it and making it adequate to the times. In an excellent brief presented to a joint committee of parliament in January, 1967, the Professional Institute of the Public Service made this point strongly. They hold this view even more emphatically today in the prevailing economic atmosphere.
Some of the figures advanced in support of their case before that committee bear repetition today. For instance, experience indicates that federal public servants who retire at age 65 live, on the average, for another 14 years. Those who retire at 60 live for 17 more years. About 20 per cent of public servants live 20 and more years following retirement. In view of the advances continually being made in health and medicine, this period of life may be expected to increase, not decrease.
In 1949 a pension of $150 a month was considered reasonable, if not princely. Today, 20 years later, it barely pays the rent. Many of the 20 per cent of pensioners who retired in the 1949 era are still eking out an existence on pensions too often well below even the $150 figure. Surely, Mr. Speaker, social justice and common decency demand that the real value of the pension, in terms of current purchasing power, should be maintained for these public servants. They should not be penalized by society for having been born 20 years too soon nor, I believe, should their career of service to the country be set so cheap as to condemn them to degradation and want.
What justification can there be for denying them all the benefits of all the advances achieved since their retirement? As a good employer, and as the exemplar of the rights and protection of the individual within a just society, the government should ensure that their retirement benefits are automatically adjusted to the increased costs of Canadian life.
The old system of adjusting government pensions has obviously failed to meet the need. We should now consider some means of making post-retirement adjustments that will achieve the objective of the superannuation plan, which is to provide retired public servants with a standard of living related to the standard enjoyed prior to retirement. Whatever means we choose to accomplish this, it cannot be of the periodic review type where 21362-9J
DEBATES	127
The Address-Mr. McIntosh action can come only after need has far outstripped the remedy. To help reach this desirable objective, those most intimately concerned with it, the public servants covered by superannuation, must have a voice. That is why I claim superannuation must be negotiable at the bargaining table.
In a number of other countries pensions are a proper topic for negotiation. The federal civil service retirement system of the United States has a cost of living increase formula linking pensions with the consumer price index. Our aim must be to provide the same justice to Canadian public servants, to ensure that there is automatic adjustment to meet changed economic conditions. I realize that such a formula would entail additional cost, but this cost does not necessarily have to be an additional burden on general government expenditure.
I was pleased, Mr. Speaker, that I was in the House this afternoon to listen to the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) when he tried to explain the reason that this session of parliament might be called the "white paper session". He said that we in the opposition criticized but offered no alternatives, and he also implied that our suggestions would create additional expenditures. I had intended to deal at length with some of the statements he made, but I was pleased to note that immediately after he sat down the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) rose to his feet and answered all the statements that I had intended to answer.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I was amazed when I heard the statement, which has been made several times during the course of this debate, that the cost of the present Prime Minister's staff is twice that of his predecessors, $350,000 a year compared with $150,000 a year for Mr. Pearson and $50,000 a year for the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). The number of elite advisers to the government has reached the astronomical figure of 117, at a cost of $1.5 million.
These are some of the things, Mr. Speaker, for which we criticize this government. It is not our position to tell them how to run their business. We offered alternatives to the general public in 1968 that were not accepted. The solutions offered by the present government were accepted, and what does the public of Canada find today? They find the government has no answers, that they want a session full of white papers by means of which


The Address-Mr. McIntosh they can study today's problems. What have they been doing for the last 18 months? They were supposed to know the solutions. The Liberals told the people of Canada that they knew what the solutions were before they took office. All opposition parties, and quite rightly so, criticized them for the inaction that will become apparent during the next 12 months, the term of this session. They say now they do not know what the answers are but will study the problems. I would say that those members of the general public of Canada who put their cross on the ballot for the present government will long remember, and one wonders whether they will do it again.
I want to say that the problem I am dealing with at the present time does not entail expenditures for the present government or the public of Canada. There appears to be sufficient earning power within the fund itself to offset any additional cost. This additional cost could be offset to a large extent, if not entirely, if the government were to bring the superannuation account into the economic world of today. Civil servants have advocated this course since 1967 when they presented their last brief.
The government should credit the superannuation account with interest at rates somewhat closer to those prevailing elsewhere throughout the economy. Private employers can invest pension funds in a manner calculated to offset increased payments and adjustments. The government cannot. But it could increase the superannuation account interest rate from 4 per cent to a more realistic figure. As things now stand, public servants are forced to lend money to the federal government through superannuation payment deductions at a rate of 4 per cent. In view of conditions prevailing outside this captive fund, this is little short of highway robbery and, I am certain, would not be condoned in any other joint venture unless one party had dictatorial control over the fund, such as the government has over the superannuation account, superannuation account.
Even the latest issue of Canada Savings Bonds yields 8 per cent at maturity and interest rates on other investments sold in the open market are even higher. Today, reference has been made to outside groups which are paying 9 per cent on borrowed money. Savings accounts in chartered banks constitute a far better investment bet today than does the federal superannuation account, yet

public servants have no choice. It is this to which I object. Civil servants have no voice or control over this account.
Funds are borrowed from the Canada Pension Fund at rates approaching 7 per cent- last year it was 6.92 per cent-and the unemployment insurance fund sells bonds at comparable rates. Yet the superannuation fund, fed by a compulsory flow from a captive army of public servants, yields a pitiable 4 per cent. The province of Ontario pays 6 per cent on a comparable fund. Why can the federal government not do the same thing?
In the 11 years to 1968, the superannuation account increased nearly three times to close to $3 billion. This was $3 billion which the federal government had at its disposal at the bargain rate of 4 per cent-$3 billion that, in effect, public servants were forced to lend to the government. They had no alternative. They were forced to lend this money to the government which, in its wisdom, saw fit to pay them 4 per cent when the government would have had to pay at least 8 per cent, according to the last bond issue, to borrow money from the general public. What made the phenomenal growth of the fund possible was the fact that in every one of the 11 years contributions exceeded payments-certainly an indication that these payments did not keep abreast of the rising cost of living. In 11 years the account earned over $648 million dollars in interest, at 4 per cent. Had a rate similar to Ontario's 6 per cent been effective there would have been $324 million more in earnings available to meet pension adjustment payments. In other words, 50 per cent more would have been put into that fund if the federal government had paid the same rate of interest on their superannuation fund as the province of Ontario.
The account paid out $509 million over 11 years, while taking in $531 million over the same period, without touching any of the original investment. What would $324 million additional have meant to retired public servants in those years if it had been paid out as an adjustment on the cost of living? In other words, taking these figures roughly, if there had been an adjustment clause in this account, civil servants on pension would have enjoyed at least a 50 per cent higher standard of living.
The superannuation account consists of public servants' own money, but it is at the disposal of the government, and entirely controlled as to earning power and use by the
October 27, 1969	COMMONS
government. Little wonder that public servants today are crying out for some voice in the handling of their own fund. On the face of these figures I have quoted, the government may have been smart in its own, narrow field of financing but it has been guilty of gross mismanagement of the fund in the interests of its contributors and in neglecting the best of interests of public servants. The least we can do now is to adjust the superannuation account interest rate to something like the government's long-term bond yield.
We must act to make sure that provisions are made for automatic adjustment of the pensions of retired public servants to the cost of living. In order to arrive at an acceptable and fair method of doing this, the superannuation system of the federal government should be made negotiable between employees and their employer.
There is a wider field of possibilities lying beyond this basic need, Mr. Speaker. They are possibilities that any government genuinely interested in people and professing concern, such as this government does, for the individual Canadian in a just society would be wise to explore. For instance, there is the question of making funds available from the superannuation account for housing loans to public servants. There is the urgent question of improvement in widows' pensions. There is the question of control of the fund by joint committee of representatives of the employer and employees, and the possibility of investment beyond the present narrow confines imposed by the present Act.
I think this House should be given the opportunity of overhauling the Public Service Superannuation Act thoroughly, if not in all its particulars then, certainly, in a few specific instances. I am not interested at the moment in trying to apportion blame for the past "victimization" of Canada's public servants, but I do believe that they have been victimized by the arbitrary nature of the legislation and the operation of the supperan-nuation account exclusively by the government. Let us now have a little participatory democracy. Let us allow the public servants of Canada to have a little say in how their money is handled and how their retirement position can be improved. I would ask that the Prime Minister give meaning to some of the words he uttered in this House on Friday when he stated that his government's primary responsibility is to the people of Canada. The figures offered by some other members of this House have shown him how the cost of
