The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc operating his office has risen since 1963 from $50,000 a year to $350,000 a year. I wish he would give the same consideration to the Public Servants who have served this country well and whose costs have also increased, although not in the same proportion. I think in this regard he should practice what he preaches.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Referring to another group in our society, the Prime Minister said this on Friday: There is no need anywhere in Canada for misguided or misinformed zealots to resort to acts of violence in the belief that only in this fashion can they accomplish change.
He went on to say:
Those who would defy the law and ignore the opportunities available to them to right their wrongs and satisfy their complaints will receive no hearing from this government.
I ask the Prime Minister, the members of the cabinet and, in particular, the minister present, what opportunities will be given to our public servants to right their wrongs and satisfy their complaints in connection with their superannuation fund. I hope there is some plan of action. If there is any substance to the Prime Minister's speech, and if he is genuinely concerned with unrest and discontent among certain groups in our society, I suggest this is one area where he can immediately demonstrate that there are other means that can accomplish change, right wrongs and satisfy complaints. This is one area where one word from the Prime Minister will rectify this injustice.
Many of us in the opposition are only too well aware that it is unwise to listen to what the Prime Minister says. We are much better informed if we watch what he does. I am sure that many thousands of Canadians who once had faith in the just society will be watching for immediate action to be taken by this government on this issue.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to give my modest appreciation of the Speech from the Throne and to indicate what I believe to be the views of my constituents as regards the policies expressed therein.
While listening to His Excellency the Governor General last Thursday, we could, once more, observe that the ultimate goal sought by the government is always to provide more happiness to every Canadian citizen. In fact,


The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc the government, the Liberal party, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) give more and more importance to the respect due to the human being. Their primary concern is the welfare, security and liberty of each citizen, and they have expressed that concern with remarkable clarity and vigour in the Speech from the Throne.
During the first session, before beginning to carry out its program of justice, the government thought it advisable to revitalize its proposed legislation and to improve its working tools, particularly, the parliamentary procedure. Although it was not an easy thing to do, and of limited interest to the general public, this has nevertheless been completed.
All the legislation passed during the first session as well as the preliminary work done to prepare this new session, have been summarized in a Speech from the Throne of a new type. We consider this speech as a most happy initiative taken by the government, an initiative that deserves to be praised.
All the realizations listed in this speech, whether the Official Languages Act, the reorganization of the government, the measures to control inflation and to protect the consumer, to name only a few of them, are for the government the assurance of a successful session to come.
Now, it is generally anticipated that because of the austerity program which is going to prevail for an indefinite length of time in order to reduce the threat of inflation, the government will insist on a certain stability of the administrative structures, on simplifying the administration to ensure greater efficiency within the federal departments, services and programs. This concern for efficiency seems to be, at present, the government's top priority. We can but approve because it is wise nowadays to be very cautious before launching any large scale undertaking.
There is, however, a very happy exception to this austerity program, namely the projects of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion whose budget is to be increased, which would make this department the main weapon in the fight against social, economic and regional disparities. We are delighted, my constituents and myself, that the Rimouski constituency, which I have the honour to represent in the house, is in the pilot regional development area of the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe peninsula. This is why we have set our hopes on the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand), in charge of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion

which he heads with efficiency and in a masterly way.
That is why the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) surprises me a little, as it must surprise many among us. As I read it, it says that the government intends to stall action to eliminate what I would summarize by the word "poverty" in some areas of our country.
It seems to me that this priority, as spelt out in the Speech from the Throne, is an answer to the question of the Leader of the Opposition.
Some members of the opposition along with those who are against the government and the Liberal party may criticize the Speech from the Throne, saying that, like all government programs, it is insignificant and does not contain anything spectacular to draw public attention and prompt editorialists or radio and television commentators to engage in written or oral analyses. Yet, it was not so long ago when major statements were made and, rightly or wrongly, they were described as shattering. About two months ago, the Prime Minister explained his position on austerity and efficiency measures taken by the government to streamline administrative structures and fight inflation. He also explained, on October 19, the attitude that the government might take in connection with the management of certain Crown corporations, for instance the C.B.C.
Following those statements, I believe that the majority of Canadians approved the Prime Minister, while admiring his qualities of true leader, and especially his great frankness, and, particularly, that integrity of mind peculiar to him.
The Speech from the Throne is nothing but a preamble, a foreword characterized by its brevity and its clarity. Some will perhaps say that it is not complete, that it gives a very vague idea of what the legislation program of this session will be.
I think it is the opposite considering the list of the titles of the bills that the Prime Minister tabled in the house before the moving of the Address in reply. According to me, the list is the practical complement of the legislative program outlined in the Speech from the Throne. Indeed, is it not an appropriate answer to the questions some could ask? Is it not the concrete expression of our program of activities for this new session? Does not each


title of those bills relate to Canadian priorities?
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
During the parliamentary recess-although the word conveys the wrong impression because members from all parties undoubtedly saw to their duties during that period while members of the Cabinet continued to govern the country-some people have been working, judging from the list of bills and the impending publication of White Papers on most important matters, such as fiscal reform, social security and foreign affairs.
This indicates that White Papers will be increasingly used to inform Canadians in advance on priority questions of interest to them and to invite them to make their views known. Anyone can see that there are priorities in Canada and that the government has undertaken to determine them quite accurately.
As for reforms concerning individual rights, we have noted the proposal for lowering the voting age to 18. If it is implemented, it will hopefully result in encouraging more people to take an interest in federal politics.
We have also noted the government's desire to amend again the Criminal Code in order to restrict the use of wire-tapping and other eavesdropping devices for a better protection of the rights and privacy of the individual.
The government is still concerned with the problems that interest the people to the highest degree, like housing. This seems to be the third priority set by the government. As a matter of fact, in spite of the threats posed by inflation, and the need for an austerity program, the government has set as its objective to build in a five-year span one million houses and dwellings likely to meet the needs of low-income families.
With the same principles underlying its programs, it plans to protect the consumers even further, to undertake an in-depth reform of the unemployment insurance scheme, to improve labor-management legislation and to check water pollution.
If it cares for the problems confronting the people, the government does not care less for those where the people are less directly involved, as, for instance, the revamping of the Constitution which is one of its priority projects.
Far from forgetting this problem of the Constitution, the government is giving it greater importance and will spare no effort to
The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc make this important revision successful. Therefore we have here a fourth priority.
We also see that the government remains mindful of international politics, to take stock on these questions, to put things in order. The session has scarcely started, but we will all have many opportunities to come back on the plans outlined in the Speech from the Throne.
At this point, I am pleased to join my colleagues who have approved and congratulated the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Both have discharged their duties with much thoroughness and grace. The hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) stated brilliantly his views and those of his fellow-citizens concerning Canada's main problems, our role as members of parliament and the question of poverty in our affluent society.
On the other hand we noted very enthusiastically that the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) recalled to us the importance of the Saguenay, his region. Talking with much spirit and verve he described the region and told us of its history in a very colourful style.
These two members have certainly done justice, not only to their constituents but also to all of us who sit in this house. That is why, falling in stop with several other hon. members, I wholeheartedly, support and congratulate them.
Many people in Canada where very much interested in the Speech from the Throne, and so were, I am sure, my constituents. The citizens of my area, Mr. Speaker, cannot but develop a keen interest in our activities and welcome the program announced in the Speech from the Throne, mainly because of the priorities stated in it, namely, those related to the budget and to the projects of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. However, I am sure that they have their own views on these programs to which they will contribute constructive criticism.
A few months ago, the citizens of the pilot area of the Lower St. Lawrence, the Gaspe Peninsula and the Magdalen Islands to which belons the population of the Rimouski riding I have the great honour of representing, decided to engage into an era of planning. In the meantime, the latter was high lighted by two historical dates; May 1967, in the course of which was set up at Chandler, the Regional council for the development of Eastern Quebec and May 1968, during which the representatives of both the Quebec government and the government of Canada, signed


The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc at Rimouski the general agreement on Canada-Quebec co-operation, an agreement which has to do with the first five-year plan of the expansion program drafted by a nonprofit corporation, the Eastern Quebec Development Board.
My fellow-citizens in the pilot area were happy to see, in 1967, the setting up of a body which would become their spokesman with the Eastern Quebec Regional Development Board and in that capacity a valuable inter -locuter, ready to accept their representations; but all the happier in 1968 when the federal-provincial agreement was signed which provided for some $260 million to be spent over a five-year period on developing their economy and thus improving their lot.
Since then, that is in the last 17 months or so, under the terms of that agreement, things have been done, steps have been taken in various fields such as agriculture, fishing, forestry, tourism, urban development, transportation; the national park at Forillon is not the least of those measures. In fact, it represents quite an accomplishment in which all will rejoice when the time comes to really develop tourism in that huge area of Canada.
I must, however, take this opportunity to say that the local people and the Regional Development Council have been quite concerned with regard to the setting up, the improvement of the infrastructure of the services and other instruments essential to the industrialization of the pilot area; and I believe that they are becoming increasingly concerned, and rightly so. The chairman of the Regional Development Council has stated repeatedly that the development project for eastern Quebec would be a complete failure unless everything was done to ensure the growth of existing viable industries and to promote the establishment of new industries capable of creating new employment, social and economic staibility and progress.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I believe that those words were both sensible and timely. My fellow-citizens know that it is incumbent on them, first of all, to see to it that such words are constantly translated into action, both by them and by the government. That is when they rely more and more on the assignment given the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and his officials, on their vitality and vigilance.
The traditional tasks and undertakings should no more be financed through the special appropriations provided under some

agreement. Nor for our own good and that of the country, should the role of the pilot area and its people be that of a Guinea-pig only. It should evolve normally, all the experiments should be carried out within the pilot area and the local citizens should be allowed to share in them. Speaking about the necessary infrastructure of industrialization one normally implies urbanization, housing policy and services as well as functional industrial parks, adequate seaports, railway and air services and industrial promotion.
Recently, some joint intermunicipal urbanization boards were established, in order to urbanize specific areas selected by the Eastern Quebec Development Board. In my opinion, the first commission, or one of the first to have been established in the area, is the one covering Rimouski-Mont-Joli-Prince in the constituency which I represent, the most highly populated community in the area.
This commission has quite a heavy task to perform, and it is agreed that it will be unable to discharge it without the financial assistance of the government.
As for functional and modern industrial parks equipped with all the necessary facilities and sidings, it is obvious that it is in the first place a municipal and provincial responsibility, but following newly adopted legislation, the federal government has a great responsibility in that field, whence the importance of the most perfect accord in that regard between the three levels of government.
A federal-provincial committee on transport was recently formed to determine the necessity and ways of improving the transportation system, in order to answer the needs that will arise when other programs of the plan are carried out. It aims at preparing a program for the establishment of an integrated transportation system and at judging the impact other programs of the plan had on communication networks.
It has been said recently that this territory has numerous harbor facilities and even excessive equipment in that field, without a rational utilization. Let us hope that the study of the commission will rationalize those structures. People in my riding are somewhat worried about this and are greatly interested in the commission's work. We all hope we will keep intact what we have acquired in nearly a century.
We want a rational improvement of what we have and here I refer especially to the


Port of Rimouski-wharves of Pointe-au-Pere and Rimouski East-which until now has been the most profitable one in the area. That modern seaport is a multi-purpose one. It may serve industry as well as agriculture. I refer here to the transportation of goods in general and to the ferry services. Year round navigation is relatively easy in our area, in the lower St-Lawrence, along the coasts, where ice is broken easily during winter time.
Seaports in industrial and urban areas must be kept in working order at all times and ready to play their part fully, especially in the industrial field.
Air services are also important. The existence however of a regional airport in the pilot area-the Mont-Joli airport-should not bring about the closing down of local airports already existing but provide for their continuation for the benefit of local transports in the Gaspe peninsula, in the lower St. Lawrence and on the north shore. The Rimouski .airport should in this field remain the local (airport.
The difficulties faced by farmers in my constituency are not too different in principle from those faced by the farmers in Canada as a whole, except that farmers in our area have to put up with the various options resulting from the intensive development of our territory.
First, there is their low income, a very hard problem to solve. Our farmers are worrying more and more about agricultural or semiagricultural concerns, too small to be economical, about the unsteadiness of price yield and hence of the agricultural income, about regional disparities which seem to be increasing. Perhaps their greatest problem is the increase of the production cost, which goes hand in hand with the reduction of the selling price.
The marketing problems, the continuing decline of our rural communities, the problems raised by our markets and our international exchanges our frequent surpluses in farm products affect them also to the highest degree.
We should help them find other skills; it might be in this area that a better use of our agricultural research is most necessary for them. They too produce or can produce more than the demand requires. Finally, in spite of the praise-worthy effort in that direction for the past few years, they would have an increasing need for retraining. In fact, they would have an increasing need for means of 21362-10
The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc improving their knowledge of the agricultural technology and their general training.
While a systematic effort was being made in order to reorganize our farmers in their main specialty, the dairy industry, and while it was decided to increase their production to such a level that their operation would become economical, the government at the same time had to legislate on the production quotas at the national level. However, it would have been very useful to our farmers to enjoy then a regional quota. That would have been logical and reasonable, I think even in the framework of a national policy, in view of the fact that those farmers lived in a pilot area recognized by the government.
In any event we can indeed say and think that the government has a very well thought out agricultural policy. However, because of the very serious problems of the agricultural class, it will ensure that next year, following the report that must be presented shortly by the Commission of Agricultural Planning, be a year of careful examination of the status of the farmer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate in the hush of expectancy in this great chamber with a large and attentive audience. I am pleased to note that in the last five minutes five more members on the government side have come in, increasing their total membership in the House by 50 per cent. I congratulate them on their perspicacity, as mentioned by the Minister of Manpower, and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen), who is here at this particular time.
Let me also congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. As my friend the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) said, I am sorry that the mover was not a sufficiently powerful advocate to persuade more of his fellow members to pay attention to what he said. I hope, however, they will read, inwardly digest and take some encouragement from his remarks.
I want to congratulate the seconder. I had the pleasure of serving with him on what I considered to be a very important committee which dealt with statutory instruments. I am satisfied that his committee made a very momentous advance in dealing with parliamentary traditions in this House. It brought forward a revolutionary document. This is something for which 1 and some other members have been working for a number of years. I was very happy that my advocacy, coupled with certain pressures a year ago, was effective and I was successful in persuading the government to set up this committee. I am firmly of the opinion that it will have a very considerable impact on the workings of this parliament.
I believe that far into the future, beyond that time when the impact of many bills to be placed before us and considered will have diminished, the effect of this committee's work, in the sense that it brings a real measure of participatory democracy to the people of this country, will continue. This will assist members of this house in dealing with these tremendous problems which face all of us in western democracies. More than 90 per cent of the measures which affect the people in a

democracy are those that are not seen in the form of legislation but rather in the form of orders-in-council and regulations. I do not intend to use this occasion to establish my position in this debate. As was indicated by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), we will have an opportunity to do so later on.
I should also like to congratulate the two hon. members who have become Ministers without Portfolio. This increases the number of cabinet members to 30. In passing, I note that it is of some interest that this matter of inflation has finally reached the cabinet.
Let me also congratulate the three hon. members who have been promoted to the position of parliamentary secretary. They have now taken one step closer to the real position of power. I am sure they will distinguish themselves in the particular areas of responsibility to which they have been assigned.
It is my intention to say something about this matter of the Speech from the Throne and this debate. In view of the fact that we are at this time enjoying a parliamentary siesta, hon. members are not here in large numbers. In my opinion, this should continue to be a very important debate. Hon. members in all parts of the house have now returned from their constituencies. They should be bringing here the sense of the urgency they felt in respect of certain problems during the course of their peregrinations.
It has been my experience in the almost 12 years I have been here that this is the time when problems should be put to the house in order that, through the processes of democracy, solutions can ultimately emerge on to the legislative assembly line. If, as a result of discussions with the people at home, an hon. member has an idea he feels should be ventilated in this House, it is during the throne speech debate that he has the first opportunity to do so.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
While I do not expect all ministers and government backbenchers-nor for that matter all the opposition members-to be here, I think this is a time and place when members should be present in much larger numbers, particularly government members, to take heed of what is being said. Some hon. members on the government side have suggested that the backbenchers, particularly those on


the opposition side, are not offering any constructive suggestions. I suggest to these hon. members that they read between the four corners of the debate on the Speech from the Throne, where they will find suggestions advanced from time to time as a means to alleviate some of the distress which hangs over this country and as a means to deal with some of the problems which we all know exist. There is a multitude of proposals, all of which cannot, of course, be accepted by the government but which could be considered, properly refined and some of them used. If this is not to be the case, we might well consider doing something else with the time now being used in the Throne Speech debate.
Let us think of something important. For example, I have on the order paper a proposal that some means should be found by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to deal with private members' bills. I think probably the most flagrant hypocrisy we have in this house is that members public bills are advanced year after year, debated for a time limit of one hour and then sent back into the limbo from which they emerged. In my view it should be the practice here, as it is in the United Kingdom, Australia and most democracies, that for a limited number of such bills there should be an opportunity to test the feeling of the House. A vote should be taken on some of them-I do not suggest on all of them-so that we can evaluate the efforts of hon. members who have laboured, made an intensive study of an idea and brought forward a private member's public bill. They should have the right, at least during the course of a parliament, to have their bills put to the question in the House. This does not, of course, mean that the government must accept them. The government may not be ready for them. Some bills may involve a point of view that is repugnant to the philosophy of the government-if one can find a government which has a philosophy-or they may involve the expenditure of money which the government may feel is not within its scope at the time. But at least the government would be put on the spot and would have to take a stand. I would have to use the Whip to call in its members to vote against bills which some government members have introduced.
If we cannot make better use of the time spent on this type of debate, I suggest this as an alternative. I say, in answer to those members on the government side who have been

The Address-Mr. Baldwin critical of the opposition for not offering constructive suggestions, that they should read well what has been said by opposition members during the debate on the Speech from the Throne; they should read the amendments which opposition members have put forward from time to time during the course of the debate, and they should read the private members resolutions Which are advanced. There have been suggestions that the Speech from the Throne is part of a carefully planned scheme of this government. In order to erase any doubt as to my position may I say that I agree wholeheartedly with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in his description of the speech from the Throne as nothing but a stalling device. The apologists for the government, those who attempt to rationalize its position and the plodding, pedestrian passage of this government, turning the Prime Minister from a go-go dancer to an exponent of the Hesitation Waltz during the course of 18 months, have their explanation for this. I understand those members of the press who are in reality really an extension of the Liberal propaganda machine which have a duty to do and have performed it well within the limits of their ability. They have rushed with loud whinnies of explanation into a rationalization of this conduct. What has dumbfounded me is the less irresponsible part of the media which has bought this doctrine.
What is this three year doctrine or plan? The first year it was to carry out the mandate of the Pearson administration, follow the program and put into effect all the pieces of chewed-up legislation which were not completed. My answer to that is simple; I could say "nuts". I shall go further, however, and deal with it. I tell the people that 14 members of the present cabinet were members of the previous administration, and I believe, 24 members of the cabinet were supporters of the previous administration. The programs, policies and legislation advanced by the previous administration must have had their support; they must have supported them both in and out of the House. It is quite irrational for them now to say with an appearance of reluctance that they were compelled to do this. Even if you do not accept that point of view, in June, 1968, an election was held and the Prime Minister secured what he had asked for, namely, a majority government; the first majority government in this House

Mr. Baldwin for ten years. Since the Prime Minister had this mandate there was no necessity for him to carry out any part of the program of the previous administration if he did not believe in it, if his supporters on the government benches did not believe in it and if his ministers did not believe in it.
I suggest there were many other things which should have had priority, and there was no reason at all for the Prime Minister, his followers and the people in this cabinet- the professional procrastinators who follow along with him-not to go ahead and deal with the problems and priorities which now have come into focus. That was the first year. In the second year, what do they say? The second year is the year of white papers, the year in which they will bring forward suggestions and set wheels in motion through the machinery of government to find out what the people are thinking. We do not have very much time left to deal with some of the very serious and difficult problems which we face. I am an advocate of the use of white papers. There is a time and a place for submitting to the legislative examination of hon. members of this House ideas which at a later date can be incorporated into the policies and financial programs necessary to make life better for the people of this country. But there must be a time element involved. A period of at least two years must be involved in this process. A white paper must be submitted at least two years before the legislation is required obviously, the white papers of this year may become the legislation of next year, and that will be the last year of the three-year program. The third year will be the year of legislation. Then we will be ready for an election, when the legislation is still fresh on the statute books and not yet brought into effect to a degree where it could have any apparent benefit to the people.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
This is not the way in which a responsible, democratic government should be acting. It is more in the line of a classical Liberal pattern of deceit, delay and confusion. There are those who say that the Prime Minister is not really a Liberal. I say he is, and I think he and the Liberal party deserve each other. I make the point that there is no doubt that the right hon. Prime Minister is a Liberal. It is rather a question of the date of the Liberalism which he follows. Some of my friends suggest he is a Mackenzie King Liberal; others take him back as far as Gladstone. But I

DEBATES	October 27, 1969
think you have to go back a little farther than that. I would go back to the time of Genghis Khan and fit him into those times.
It would be bad enough if all this procrastination, delay and confusion took place in normal times, but these are not normal times. Today we have face serious, difficult problems such as inflation. It is just called inflation if you are in the carriage trade, but if you are of the class of people who are really hurt by it-the class of people to whom our amendment is addressed-inflation means a rise in the cost of living, a rise in the price of milk and bread and an increase in the cost of renting accommodation. All these are problems which bear very seriously upon men and women of below average income. They are the ones who are the sufferers. They are the people who are being hurt desperately and to whom inflation is not something which you can absorb, not something you can pass along to customers and to people with whom you deal. They are the people to whom inflation is, in fact, a major tragedy. This, of course, compelled our party to move the type of amendment we did.
There is also the problem of welfare and social adjustment, the problems of housing, of transportation and of the urban sprawl which has now confronted us. These problems compelled the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hel-lyer) to part company with his leader and the cabinet. He did not think that the position being taken by them could in any sense provide reasonable and rational solutions. There is the problem of industrial unrest. There is the problem of unemployment, 'and social problems such as the use of drugs, pollution and civil disorder. There are also problems connected with our native peoples, problems of regional disparity and those of agriculture.
I could speak for some time on the problem which affects my constituency and all parts of northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan, that is, regions afflicted by the inability last year to market the grain which the farmers produced and the difficulty of harvesting this year because of incredibly bad weather. In many oases less than 25 per cent of the crop was harvested. The government was unable to offer any reasonable suggestion which would be of benefit to these farmers.
There will be other opportunities to speak about this problem in the House, but I take the time now to indicate to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), to the Prime Minister and to the Minister without Portfolio charged with the responsibility of the Wheat

Board (Mr. Bang), that I and members of this party will not rest until the government has done something to solve the problem. Each day these matters will be brought to the attention of the government, and it will either act or stand exposed to the people of Canada in all the nakedness of their legislative program.
These problems exist. They exist, of course, in many other countries in the western world, but I think they are aggravated here because we have a federal system. A federal system is brought into existence because of geographic and economic diversities in the country. It is therefore essential to have a central government and regional governments. But the federal government structure and the problems which exist in that structure are exaggerated in Canada because of ethnic, cultural and linguistic distinctions.
It is not good enough, as this government would have us believe, to delay and to stall for three years. In three years it will be too late. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that many of the problems which four years before loomed a little more than a cloud on the horizon have now become a great storm hovering over us. In 1972 they will have dissipated their energy and destruction over the whole country. I very much fear that if the government intends, because of the three year plan, to delay taking serious action in regard to some of the problems I have indicated, the people of this country should take heed of the consequences.
There is the question of our national unity. The other day the Prime Minister made a speech which he has followed on one or two occasions. He has been praised by some members of the press and by other people. He has been praised by his own party. I go along with him when he says that there should be no place in democracy for violence, that there should be no place in our system of working out our problems amongst ourselves, in complete, for taking to the streets with bombs and devastation. However, unfortunately, when people have been denied for so long many of the things to which they consider they are entitled, they resort to the power of protest. We have seen this in the United States, in France and in Germany, and we are beginning to see it in Canada. So while I agree with what the Prime Minister said in this respect, I do not think that this alone is enough. There will be protest, and people will take to the streets; there will be demonstrations until the problems which cause the

The Address-Mr. Baldwin demonstrations and protest have been, if not eliminated, at least the subject of meaningful attention and a reasonable attempt has been made to deal with them.
There is talk of separatism in the province of Quebec. All of us deplore separatism, whether it is in Quebec, British Columbia, Alberta or any part of this country. We all believe that we have made in the northern part of the North American continent a rather unique attempt to bring people from various countries together with our two founding peoples and with the native population. We have attempted to work out a means of living together in peace and harmony with a common national interest. It is difficult, even under the best of circumstances, when these distinctions exist. Last May I was in Strasbourg attending meetings of the Council of Europe. I was fascinated by what I was told by my colleagues, by officers of the commission and the Court of Human Rights. I was told by the registrar of a case which had been dealt with by the commission and then tried in the court which dealt with the problems of language rights in Belgium. When you have these racial and cultural distinctions in a country you are bound to have problems, and I do not think you will ever completely eliminate them.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Added to these problems are those of economic disparity, of unemployment, of the inability of people to find housing and all the concurrent difficulties which crowd into great urban metropolitan areas such as we have in Toronto and Montreal. When we consider the difficulties in connection with the process of education and these are added to the other problems which face us, we realize it will take a great deal of hard work and effort to reach solutions. The effort must be made in a way that will convince the people who have these problems that they are known, that their problems are being attended to, or at least that a serious effort is being made to do so. I do not think the Prime Minister's speech affected one person in the province of Quebec who believed that the way for Quebec lay in separatism. That is not the way to do it. The way to deal with it is in this House and in the council chambers of the cabinet. If the Prime Minister thinks otherwise, then I think he is completely wrong. Deal with the serious economic problems and you have dealt with, separation.


The Address-Mr. Baldwin
Oftentimes the Prime Minister and the government remind me of a doctor sauntering along a lane to attend a patient, exchanging philosophical quips with the people on each side of him, and by the time he gets to the man's house he finds the patient is dead. I fear this will be the situation here. It is all very well to take a tough line; it is all very well to talk as the Prime Minister talked, but by itself it is not enough. Quite sincerely I urge the Prime Minister, the members of his cabinet, and other supporters of the Prime Minister and the government to ensure that before this session is over we get away from some of the trivia on the order paper. I am not saying they are parts of a legislative program which are not needed-probably all of them are needed-but there is the question of urgencies and priorities.
There is the question of the cost of living. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has at least five bills to introduce, including a uniform packaging and labelling bill. What will we have from that? Will we have the minister on a television program telling housewives how to order goods, stressing to new mothers the virtues of standard size Flush-a-Bye disposable diaper? Is this the legislative program with regard to consumer problems? Something more than that is needed, Mr. Speaker. These problems require a concerted effort. Time has stolen from the federal government the opportunity to act. Time will not permit this government, this parliament and the provincial legislatures to work out in a calm, deliberate way methods of changing the constitution whereby we will have a better division of powers so that each sector will in its own tidy way be able to deal with the problems. There will have to be concerted action. This means that the government and 11 legislatures will have to say, "We must accept a concerted, pragmatic attack on specific issues." This involves a measure of harmony amongst the legislatures and the government which does not exist today.
When the Prime Minister goes to Montreal and makes a political speech at a political dinner, savagely attacking the government of Quebec and the administration of the city of Montreal, when the president of the Liberal party goes to the province of Nova Scotia and makes a scurrilous attack on the government of that province, when the federal government before the end of the last session successfully forces down the throats of provinces such as Alberta and Ontario a type of medicare program which was not acceptable to

them, and when the federal government fails to deal with the problems of agriculture in western Canada, how can there exist the harmony necessary for all the government officials involved to sit down and say, "These problems are urgent and essential. We must get together. We must forget the constitution. We must in a constructive way attack the problems of pollution, the problems of inflation and the problems of the large cities"?
This is the only way progress can be made, but I suggest the government has not established the necessary climate or mood. Time is running out. Time is not on our side. Therefore, I urge the government and its supporters to understand the priorities and urgencies exist today; that these problems confront the people of Canada and they must be dealt with now-they cannot wait the expiration of the three-year plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I should like to congratulate very warmly my hon. colleagues from Sarnia and Lapointe (Messrs. Cullen and Marceau) for moving the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
It is fortunate, Mr. Speaker, that at the opening of a new session, the hon. members may discourse as they like on important subjects of the Canadian life and draw the attention of the house ot the existing or eventual problems that the members will have to face or, again, who know some regions with which they are very familiar.
I suggest that the eight appointed days for the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne are intended to draw the attention of all citizens on certain problems, as I mentioned a moment ago, and to receive suggestions with respect to means of improving the laws in order to remove some disparities that are, in my view, social injustices.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The democracy in which we live makes available to us this important dialogue technique and those who took advantage of it have reaped great benefits.
Bearing this in mind, Mr Speaker, I shall try once more today to draw the attention of all the members in this house and of the government upon the problems of an urban area which lies at the feet of the national capital, that is the Hull area. As a representative of this region, if, in this house, I have


already dealt many times with its economic stagnation, it is for the simple reason that nobody seems able to understand that our problem is due to our being near Ottawa and far from Quebec.
Everybody knows that Hull is in a particular situation owing to its geographic position and its demographic composition. While we have repeated many times in this house that the Ontario-Quebec border excludes the city of Hull from the direct scope of federal authority, nobody will question the fact that Hull and its surroundings are part of a whole commonly known as the national capital area.
That is the cause of all the economic and social stagnation affecting our region since the establishment of the capital of Canada. As I said earlier, at a short distance from the capital, there is a flourishing city, a town proud of its origins, caught between two giants, the federal and provincial governments who have decided lately to wage a long-drawn constitutional war against each other.
The people who are faced with all the normal problems of a region, in addition to those coming under federal-provincial jurisdiction, incur the odium of all the fruitless quarrels that divide politicians and governments. This has prompted some fools in the province of Quebec recently to compare the city of Hull to that of Strasburg and to say that, in an independent Quebec, Hull, like Strasburg would lie at the border of another country, that is, of Canada.
Is it possible to be so narrow-minded, Mr. Speaker, as to dare mislead such an intelligent people with such a ludicrous hoax? One has only to study the history of Strasburg to realize that the population of Hull will never agree to play such a part.
I repeat that the problems which face our region are due to our proximity to Ottawa and to our distance from Quebec. Since the outbreak of this sham fight and exchange of letters, Quebec is reported to be very sensitive on the matter of territorial integrity, especially in our district located near the national capital. But while saying that territorial integrity must be preserved, this territory being in the province of Quebec but also in the national capital area, Quebec has never done anything to promote its development. Rather, they have tried to pick quarrels, and to discourage investors. Thus, no benefit is derived from the natural resources to be found in abundance in our region.
The Address-Mr. Isabelle Instead, a great many administrative structures, for which Quebec has great fondness, have been created, which, essentially, only contribute to weigh down the normal process of regional government. Through all such structures an attempt is made to solve the problem fully.
The entire problem stems from there, but it is actually only last May that the federal government announced its intention to invest large sums of money in the centre of Hull. This will promote an extraordinary economic development on the Quebec side.
It is then that ministers and high officials of the Quebec government first came to Hull in swarms as large as on the occasion of the St. Jean-Baptiste parade, in order to calm down the dissatisfaction which keeps increasing in our region. But I think that we touched the sore spot by announcing that on April 1, 1970 will be erected the first of several federal buildings in Hull. It will be built in the section which we designated as the centre of Hull. But the city of Hull and its surroundings have never been known to the rest of Quebec.
I quote at random a few examples which struck me and which I have taken down for the information of the house.
When the Quebec Professional Golfers Association held its annual tournament two years ago at the Rivermead Club, Montreal's Le Devoir, which is an extremely serious newspaper, wrote this in its sports page: Hull, Ontario.
I thought that maybe this was a mistake, but some time later a Quebec minister came to Hull and congratulated the new mayor on having defeated Miss Whitton who was then running for the Ottawa mayorship. This shows you how well people know our region.
And, on top of that, during federal-provincial conferences, the Quebec delegates and the ministers have rented luxury suites in Ottawa hotels, even though they are so proud of their province. Why did they not spend then-money in Hull, in the province of Quebec, since they brag about Quebec's know-how?
More recently, in the daily column of my good friend Henri Laperriere, of the newspaper Le Droit, it was reported that a Quebec minister of Agriculture-who once sat on the other side of the house-sent him an invitation written in English only. Quebec knows how to do things. Perhaps he thought that because the newspaper Le Droit is located in Ottawa, it must be an English paper.


The Address-Mr. Isabelle
That is how well our region is known. And that is why we are today the victims of those useless disputes over federal and provincial jurisdictions. In the province of Quebec, they court the English-speaking people in their presence, but back home, they crucify them.
In France, they act as Quebecers to show that they are independent and do not represent Canada.
In the United States they hoist the Canadian flag to make Americans believe that they are Canadians so that they can obtain capital investments, but once they return to Quebec they crucify Canada.
It is a hide-and-seek game, a drawing-room war, a match of hanky-panky and literary contests. It is in this context that our region lives and it is in this light that we have come to be known nearly everywhere in Quebec.
I would also like to say a word about the transportation system with which we must be satisfied. In fact, people from our region must pay double fare to get to work, as 50 per cent of them are employed in Ottawa.
We also suffer from various disparities, precisely because we do not enjoy the same jurisdictions on the Ontario side as in Quebec although we belong to the same economic region.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In the province of Quebec, the laws are different, which prevents many Ontarians, who are nevertheless living in the same area, to come and settle on the Quebec side. I mean the Estate Tax Act.
Outside the problem of transportation, many others prevent us from making the strides that we should have made as residents of a same area.
I believe it is the responsibility of the National Capital Commission to develop the whole district of the National Capital both on the Ontario and the Quebec sides.
If we are to establish a separate corporation to develop the district on the Quebec side in order to preserve the integrity of the territory, we will create administrative problems that will engulf us in useless debate.
In my opinion, it belongs to the National Capital Commission to develop the district, following consultations with the interested governments, and I mean the municipal authorities. In my opinion, we do not need other administrative structures to develop the district on the Quebec side.

The National Capital Commission has already been most useful, and it can still be useful if the province of Quebec is not in a position to develop the Hull district. If they lack funds as we believe it to be the case- they should rent the Hull area just as they did the area of Forillon in the Gaspe Peninsula to establish a national park.
I think that the people of Hull are tired of all those sterile discussions and that they want to live, at last, not as second-class citizens, but as equal partners like the citizens of Ottawa.
People are unhappy with the disparity in the sales tax, the transportation utilities and the estate tax between Hull and Ottawa. There is also the psychological factor which prevents people from coming to live with us because, in the province of Quebec, the unemployment rate is 7.2 per cent as compared with 3.1 per cent in Ontario and 4.9 per cent for Canada as a whole.
As to the possibility for our students to undertake university studies, it is limited to enrol at the University of Ottawa. Even there, the doors are not wide open. When vocational college graduates from the Hull area want to enter university in Quebec City or Montreal, they are told simply that there is no room except for students from the Quebec City or Montreal area. Vocational college graduates have no choice other than attending the University o>f Ottawa.
This is why ministers are mistaken when they tour our region to say it is their responsibility to develop the Quebec side, in the best interest of the province and the region. When they fail to include the Ottawa area in that region, they forget that it is one and the same economic region which cannot be cut off by a boundary, even an interprovincial boundary.
This is where I think the federal government should intervene, because the boundary is interprovincial. The government is duty bound to implement projects prepared earlier for developing the Hull area.
Today, we have to cope with technological evolution. Right now, at this very moment, there are huge traffic tie-ups at the entrances of Highways 8 and 11 leading to downtown Hull. Conditions are similar on the approaches to the Cartier-Macdonald and Chaudiere bridges simply because no traffic is allowed on the Champlain bridge which has been used for 40 years. It is just like someone who would wait to buy a new suit because the one


he is wearing is falling apart. It is normal that bridges be closed for repairs but, meantime, there are bottlenecks and motorists grow impatient.
I hope that such conditions will never be seen again, particularly if we keep in mind the magnificent tourist attractions of which our region is so proud.
I need not comment on the ski centers: Vorlage, Edelweiss, Camp Fortune, Mount St. Marie, which require better roads of access so that they may contribute to the development of Western Quebec.
In the name of the integrity of the land the federal government and the National Capital Commission are prevented from building roads. At the time the Gatineau Park was developed, we had to ask the City of Hull to expropriate on behalf of the federal government in order to prevent the Quebec government from objecting. That is the way it goes, but it is certainly no way to encourage progress and development.
In my opinion, Quebec should wake up to the tru h. Hull's situation is a case of long term agony for the Quebecers who live in an area they are so proud of. They should allow the federal government to service the land in order to improve the everyday life of the people of that area.
Mr. Speaker, the subject of bilingualism was brought up together with a lot of other things but in Quebec they are adamant in their efforts to have us accept a kind of unilingualism. Representations are made everywhere and, in my opinion, Quebec will find itself turned into a ghetto with, perhaps, civil revolution as the outcome.
Some people are not quite mature enough to realize that bilingualism is the key to a fantastic economic power. Good ideas have nothing to do with the language in which they are conveyed. Travel broadens the mind and after a while we start to wonder why we should hesitate to learn a language other than French or English since we feel the need to learn several languages.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The economic power of bilingualism opens doors in many more places than one would imagine. In Canada, we should take advantage of the fact that the national trade is split up in a proportion of 73 per cent for the English-speaking sector and 27 per cent for the French-speaking.
The Address-Mr. Isabelle
If a business in the English sector did not have French on its labels, it would lose 27 per cent of its market; on the other hand, if a business in the French sector does not have English on its labels, it runs the risk of losing 73 per cent of the Canadian market.
The Canadian market is a fantastic training ground for doing business in a language other than one's own. In addition, Canada is the only country endowed with that advantage, that of having the economic power of bilingualism, which gives it access to French-speaking and English-speaking countries throughout the world without the burden of adaptation.
The United States, the United Kingdom and France do not have that advantage.
Our education, our products, our domestic markets give us this opportunity; we should therefore take full advantage of it on international markets.
At the present time we cannot benefit fully from the exceptional power of bilingualism for various reasons; I shall not go into them now. A country must have a balanced economy throughout the land. Canada has two cultures but it must have only one economy. In a speech one of my friends made recently, he said: It is easier to build a united Canada through economy than through culture. The flag of a nation represents its culture. To fly a flag, we need a mast to represent the economy of the country.
You can easily fly two flags on the same mast but it is impossible, without tearing it up, to fly the same flag on two masts.
The key characteristic of money is that it can serve as a vehicle for understanding; to have money is less important than to know how to use it.
Trade is the common denominator of all social and political factors, of traditions, religions, cultures and languages. It is that which makes a political society.
I think that we will never make a good French Canadian out of an English Canadian just as we will not make a good English Canadian out of a French Canadian. But with both of them it is possible however, to make a very good team. Besides, we could perhaps remove from our heritage the Anglo-Saxon subtleties and the whims of Jean-Baptiste. We would then discover a common interest: the building of Canada. In my opinion, what we lacked, here, is national pride. We do not have a patriotic soul.


The Address-Mr. Isabelle
When we visit our country from one constituency to another we can only be moved by contemplating these vast territories, these fantastic national resources which are only waiting for man to put them to use. We must farm the land because this country which we love so much, we did not make people love it enough.
This is the reason why, for a few years, and despite dissensions, as we remember, we managed to endow Canada with a flag. We have got one, but we did not have time-the members of parliament being very busy as well as the governments-to generate among all Canadians, whatever their mother tongue, a national pride by showing them the beauties of the country. In my opinion, if the Canadians, between themselves, held diverging views, it is perhaps because their country was very big or because the means of transportation were lacking. Indeed, who could devote ten days to tour Canada?
Today, in the jet age, we shall know and appreciate one another much better. This is where lies, I think the whole problem of today's Canada.
With regard to economic disparities, we must be careful that our country does not get bogged down through division, whether the province of Quebec or other provinces are the cause of the splitting up because those upon whom will rest the responsibility for that division could say, as is mentioned in the Bible: "Let his blood fall upon us and upon our children." I think that in Quebec at the present time we are a little dazzled by a sort of progress which may not have been experienced for some years, thanks to men who were energetic at the beginning of the sixties but who ran out of breath because they had probably progressed too far. I still believe that Quebec will rise up again with dynamic men who will ring together again all those who want this province to remain within Confederation and who will continue to further the development of this great country of ours.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Only if the period of prosperity continues can we do the things for the poor and the needy of this country that ought to be done. I would indicate briefly to hon. members that over the past ten years we have made a great deal of progress in the area of social development in this country. We have brought into being the Canada Pension Plan, the Canada Assistance Plan, a guaranteed income for people beyond the age of 65; we have seen the implementation of medicare, and a retraining program second to none in the world has been established. I hope that we in Canada can see this development continue.
I have said before, and I repeat, that the number one problem we face in this country today is the persistent upward spiral in prices, costs and incomes. Other than this we have a prosperous and viable economy. However, unless and until we bring this spiral of inflation under effective control all the aspirations of this house toward a better life for all Canadians, all our hopes for continuous high employment, for a rising standard of living and social justice for the poor and the depressed in our country will come to naught. If rapid inflation persists, we face instead a loss of confidence in the real value of money, a serious rundown in the economy, the erosion of export markets, rising unemployment, a heavier burden upon the poor and widening divisions within our country. This is why, as I said in my budget speech, the number one task in economic policy today must be to deploy all available forces, public and private, more aggressively than ever in the battle against constantly rising prices.


I must confess to being puzzled by the position of the opposition parties. They frequently profess a great concern about this problem, particularly, and rightly so, about the effect of rapidly rising prices upon people who must live on fixed and low incomes. Yet in their participation in the debate on Friday last it seems to me that their main demand was for the government to give up the fight, or to rapidly boost expenditures in each of several dozen directions at once. Nothing at this moment could be better calculated to worsen the situation in the most desperate way.
It is important to put the matter in its true perspective. There should be no need to elaborate upon all the destructive ramifications of the kind of price increases we have been experiencing for more than three years, but it is essential to understand fully the real nature of the present situation; to understand why, despite the deployment of strong anti-inflationary policies, the situation has persisted for so long and in so acute a form. I do not think we can look at it in the light of the conventional analysis of a recurring cyclical turndown and upturn of business, production and employment.

speechtext: Who does?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is, I suggest, a major new development today. It arises from the unprecedented success we have experienced in maintaining high levels of employment and incomes throughout the post-war period, particularly over the past decade. For the first time in history we have managed to sustain an almost uninterrupted expansion of the national economy for a period of almost ten years. It is the very strength and vigour of this long economic upswing which has given such intensity and persistence to current inflationary pressures. Too many Canadians, unaware or forgetful of the principles upon which our market economy must operate, have come to expect that continuously rising incomes for everybody are now to be had as a matter of right rather than as a just reward of economic discipline, production and effort on their part.
There is another relatively new dimension to our current situation. Destructive inflation is not just a Canadian problem; rather, it is almost global in scale. In nearly every country with which we trade the rise in prices has been close to or even worse than our own. The consequences are obvious. International competitiveness is not able to exert its customary restraining influence. Instead, with
The Address-Mr. Benson some notable exceptions such as wheat, the prices of many of the goods we sell abroad have also been advancing. So too, with the prices of many of our imports. With a quarter of our total output flowing into exports, and an almost equal proportion of imports, we are inevitably caught up to some degree in worldwide inflationary pressures.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
This is not to say for one moment that we are helpless in the face of such pressure. Quite the contrary. Even if we cannot insulate ourselves from the influences of other countries, especially the United States, there is much we can do on our own account. The fact is that the sharpest rates of increase in prices, especially in recent months, have taken place in just those things for which the domestic economy is mainly responsible. This is true of most domestic services, ranging from medical fees and hospital costs to transportation services and haircuts. It is true of urban land values and housing; it is true of construction; it applies in many public services. We can and must do a better job of restraining prices and costs in all these and similar areas, and to the extent we are successful in achieving a better price performance than our trading partners we will reap rich rewards in the growth of real production and real incomes.
The broad outline of the government's policies to achieve this objective is quite clear. We have given first attention to what is called the setting of the big levers of monetary and fiscal policy. Here we have had the closest co-ordination and harmonization of policy between the government and the Central Bank. We have agreed upon the broad and interlocking strategy required in each field, with the details of program and application left to the appropriate authority. In this connection may I bring to the attention of the house the remarks on monetary policy given by the Governor of the Bank to a business conference in Toronto only last Thursday.
As for fiscal policy, the crucial decisions were taken in my first budget a year ago. At that time we adopted the tax measures necessary to assure a balance in the public accounts budget during the current fiscal year, given a normal growth of production at acceptable levels of prices. That action represented a successful shift in fiscal policy in the face of continued inflationary pressure. Last June, with further evidence of a potential overheating of the economy and renewed


The Address-Mr. Benson price pressures, we concentrated upon controlling expenditures and budgeted for a restraining surplus. In fact, as price and income increases have tended to advance more rapidly than hoped for, the federal budget is now exerting an automatic stabilizing influence and I now expect that the surplus will be significantly larger than I had forecast in my budget last year.
We are holding, and must hold, to this course notwithstanding the many appeals and urgings that we should increase government spending on many worth-while and desirable programs. I can assure hon. members opposite that there is scarcely a single item of desirable, increased spending they have mentioned which has not been argued even more forcefully and persuasively by one or more members on this side or by my cabinet colleagues. We should like very much to do the easy and popular thing-to spend freely on higher pensions, increased allowances, more subsidies for farmers and fishermen, further aid to the poor, more housing, beautifying cities, overcoming pollution, higher salaries for everyone, and so on. Believe me, over the past several years this government has done a great deal to increase expenditures on social benefits to the Canadian public. Nothing could be simpler than to spend freely on these things, and nothing would be more irresponsible. Nothing would be more damaging to the real, longer term interests of all the people these things are intended to serve. We must reject the politically expedient, short-term response and opt for a responsible fiscal policy which will contribute to the real economic health of our country and to the genuine interests and welfare of all Canadians.
We have sought, as well, to supplement fiscal policy by stimulating and encouraging the idea of voluntary restraint. There is no question that if the organized economic interest groups in our society-business, labour, professional associations, landlords, other governments-were to take a strong stand in favour of even a modest degree of restraint, and to act upon it, we would roll back the forces of inflation in very short order. The government has worked for over two years to put this idea across, and the Prices and Incomes Commission was expressly designed to help in this work. I think we have made some progress. Certainly there is a wider understanding of the issues involved, of the gains to be won by voluntary restraint, than ever before in our country. There is much

more to be done, and notwithstanding a temporary setback I am confident that the work of the commission will yield valuable results. In all of this it is absolutely vital that the government itself should show the way-and this, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made crystal clear last August, we are determined to do.
A third part of the framework of government policy against inflation concerns the regional aspect. Difficult disparities obviously complicate the task of containing inflation and maintaining high levels of employment. Monetary policy, by its very nature, must apply on a country-wide basis. There is no way, within an integrated national economy enjoying the free movement of people, goods, services and capital among all its regions, to provide for broad monetary restraint in some regions and monetary ease in others. The Central Bank, however, has always followed a policy of asking the chartered banks to keep in mind the needs of the slower growing regions whenever they find it necessary to restrict their lending and I have completely supported them in this effort.
Fiscal policy is somewhat more flexible. Even here, however, there are important limitations. The national government cannot lightly take up tax measures which seem to discriminate in favour of the taxpayers of one region or province as against those in another. As for expenditure, when total demands so far outrun revenues, as in our case, we have a clear duty to be sure that funds are provided only for genuinely worth-while projects and programs, even in lagging regions. There is no justification for simple make-work palliatives. This is all the more important because increased expenditure in the lagging regions works its way rapidly throughout the economy. Soon it adds to the intensity of demand in other regions such as southern Ontario, one of the main areas of inflationary pressure in the country.
In spite of these problems, we embarked in the last budget on certain selective measures geared to the regional aspect of the inflationary problem. Both the acceleration of the Kennedy Round tariff cuts and the temporary deferral of capital cost allowance on certain types of building in rapid-growth provinces had this purpose. Over the longer term, however, we place major reliance upon the expanding program of regional development. This is one of our highest priorities, and increasing funds are being allocated to it. There is as well the very large and rapidly
October 27, 1969	COMMONS
increasing equalization grants paid to the lower income provinces.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Perhaps I might note one aspect of the new equalization system which has assumed added significance under current inflationary conditions. The strong growth of tax revenues in the most rapidly expanding provinces also brings about a substantial increase in federal equalization grants to the less expansive provinces. These latter are thus able to finance a growth in provincial expenditure and employment-creating works even when higher spending on direct federal programs may be held back. In this fiscal year, for example, we now estimate that equalization grants to the less affluent provinces have grown by $144 million, a 25 per cent gain over the last fiscal year.
Nevertheless, regional unemployment remains as one of the most stubborn and intractable problems we must face. Reference was made last Friday to the national problem, with the rate of unemployment averaging about 5 per cent for the country as a whole. In fact, for all the provinces from Ontario to the west the rate averages out at only 3.4 per cent, well within the target range of so-called full employment. But in Quebec and eastward the unemployment rate is averaging about 8 per cent. I am satisfied that the solution to this deep-seated problem certainly does not lie in allowing inflation to rage unchecked. That would only worsen the problem. It is mainly the economically weaker regions of the country which must carry an undue share of the burden of higher costs and prices since they lack the power to win proportionate gains in income. This disparity and inequity can only be overcome by pinpointing our development effort even more selectively to accelerate basic economic growth in these regions, and this is the aim of our government.
Here the fourth part of our framework of current policies is particularly relevant. These are the policies and programs concerned with the supply or production aspects of the economy. Perhaps the broadest and most important are the expanding programs for improving manpower skills and mobility, programs on which we are spending a tremendous amount of money in this country, probably proportionately more than any other country in the world. In this regard, the steady expansion of the Department of Manpower is given a high priority, and as mentioned in the Throne

The Address-Mr. Benson Speech, new proposals for unemployment insurance will help reinforce these efforts. Similarly we have the rapid growth of our aid to the provinces for university, professional and technical education which we deem to be of great importance in our country.
I should mention as well the notable example of the very substantial government support being given to the financing of housing. Here we fully expect to again hit the target of 200,000 housing starts this year, this in the face of record high interest rates and continued extreme pressures in mortgage and financial markets. Unfortunately, even though the rate of residential building is very high, costs have continued to mount, particularly in certain centres of the country. This has certainly been one of the most unfortunate effects of the excessive rates of wage settlements which have taken place in the construction industry in several major cities across the country this year.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the minister would permit a question. I do not wish to interrupt him and could wait until he has finished. The minister speaks of the economy being overheated. Is he suggesting the inflation is due to excessive demand? Could he clarify his view with regard to this?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think I made it quite clear in what I have been saying to date. In the economy one could not say there is necessarily excessive demand, but there is a cost-price pressure at the bottom which is pushing up inflation in the economy. It would be very nice to find a simple solution to the inflation problem in the country such as the hon. member suggested last week; that is, that we adjust government spending upwards and put more pressure on the economy by creating excessive demands.
Mr. Speaker, if I may continue, it is unfortunately true that although everyone professes to be alarmed about inflation, there are important members and groups in the community who are not really deeply concerned. I would say this often includes members in the opposition. They are mainly the people who are able to exercise their economic power to stay ahead of the game. Even if their costs rise they are able to wrest proportionate and frequently greater increases in prices or incomes from the rest of the community; and if and when the crisis develops and their position is threatened, they would be the first


The Address-Mr. Benson
to come running to the government seeking help.
This is partly why, despite all our efforts, the upward spiral of prices, costs, wages and other incomes has not yet been effectively checked. 1 am the first to acknowledge this fact. Even though anti-inflationary policies have been deployed since early this year, the fires are still burning strongly in our economy. Until very recently the pace of price and wage hikes has been tending to accelerate rather than to slow down. Obviously it takes time for measures of restraint, either in the form of higher taxes or curtailed spending, to work their way through and affect the private spending decisions of individuals and business firms. There is also a large element of so-called cost-push inflation, higher costs of materials, services and wages, built into the economy going back over two or three years. I have already mentioned the impact of international inflation. All of these factors, taken together with the influence of the long economic upswing, have combined to create the great problem of deep-seated inflationary expectations. This is the expectation of people who believe that inflation will go on forever and they should get whatever they can out of it. I should like to assure the House that it is the intention of the government that this shall not happen, and it will not happen for the benefit of the little people in our country.
