The Governor of the Bank of Canada, in the speech I mentioned, has put it this way:
I do not believe that one can explain either the insistence of lenders on receiving such high interest rates or the willigness of borrowers to pay them without reference to the strong expectations of continued inflation that have developed. Borrowers have been reluctant to postpone expenditures for

fear of incurring higher costs later, and lenders; have sought to protect themselves against the impact of rising prices by refusing to lend except at high rates. Inflationary expectations have unhappily become a central feature in our economic situation, and it is a central task of economic policy to try to eliminate the causes of these expectations.
I have to say it is on this last crucial issue that I think the Economic Council of Canada has in part missed the point in their most recent annual review. I have read that document with care and I do not think that either the analysis or views of the Council are nearly so far removed from my own as has been quite loosely suggested.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
It seems to me that our differences turn out to be essentially matters of degree and not of basic principle. The Council is concerned about the dangers of excessive fiscal restraint and they focus upon the so-called lags, or the delay in the impact of policies upon the actual level of economic activity. There is, however, a further lag which the government cannot ignore. To borrow a familiar term, this is one of credibility. Governments may be slow to recognize emerging economic trends and to act upon them, but under present conditions people may also be slow to believe that the government means what it says about checking inflation. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. We cannot be sure of breaking the cycle of inflationary expectations and actual price increases until there is clear and positive evidence of a slow down in the rate of inflation in our country.
This is why we cannot afford now to ease up on the fiscal and other brakes. Indeed, I have been receiving many letters from across the whole country urging more drastic measures of control, particularly an all-out freeze on prices and wages. Most of these letters come from little people, pensioners, low wage earners, farmers and fishermen, housewives struggling to balance their household budgets; from all those, in short, who lack the economic power to bargain their incomes up as fast as prices increase. There is no doubt in their minds as to the need for all-out controls over both prices and the wage gains and fee increases they see being won by organized labour and professional groups. This is what these correspondents are asking for, rather than higher government spending and taxes in our country as proposed by members of the opposition.
I do not, of course, believe that we should resort to blanket controls except under conditions of the gravest crisis and only after other efforts have proven fruitless. Apart from the

need to secure some constitutional accord with the provinces to make controls legal, it is clear that the web of directives and controls urged by the New Democratic Party in place of fiscal and voluntary restraint would rapidly entangle the entire economy and produce stagnation,	unemploy m e nt and
inequity within our country. Let there be no mistake-if we are to control prices, there is no alternative but to control wages at the same time.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

We will continue our efforts to add to the productivity and efficiency of the economy and to seek a broader understanding as well as the co-operation of the entire community in voluntary restraint. These are the policies which will do the job for the greatest good of the greatest number of people in our country. In due course they will bring our enormously productive economy back to a firm basis for continued growth and expansion. When that prospect is firmly in sight-and we are reviewing the situation on a daily basis-we will be the first to initiate a relaxation of restraint. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with my colleagues in congratulating the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) for moving and seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. In particular I commend the seconder of the Address in Reply because I believe he has proven himself a worthy replacement for his predecessor the hon. separatist gentleman who is now deputy leader of the Parti Quebecois, and if the good of the nation requires his leadership in that constituency I trust he will have continued success.
I was a little concerned that the hon. member for Sarnia devoted much of his speech to criticizing this institution of which we are members. Even from watching the functioning of this House during the last couple of days it seems to me that what the hon. member ought to be doing is preaching more to his own caucus and less to the House. I am sure he must understand that the real strength and heartbeat of democracy radiates from this institution; therefore, we must all work together to improve its performance and efficiency. We must never lose sight of the fact that it is here that we have an opportunity to speak on behalf of those we represent, and to express opinions that are as diverse as is the nature of our country.


I also wish to congratulate the two new members of the cabinet on their appointment to office, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), but must point out that this raises the size of the Canadian cabinet to the highest it has ever been in history. I only hope their contribution might be equal to the size of the cabinet. However, I find it difficult to understand the policy of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in constantly increasing the numbers of those who assist him, whether in cabinet or in his office. One of the things which the Prime Minister has missed in his appeal for a new approach to things is the reform of the cabinet itself, which now is certainly a top-heavy organization. If the cabinet is to continue in the old pattern of things, it will not assure the kind of efficiency that the Prime Minister wants from his government.
The most impressive thing about the Speech from the Throne was the lacklustre approach it took to our problems. The public have shown an obvious lack of enthusiasm for it, even as the attitude of this House indicates to-day. I have noticed this from reading comments in the press and from contacts I have had within the past few days with various people across the nation. It is true that its positive emphasis is placed on strengthening Canadian unity, but on the other hand it promises little to meet the present day problems of Canada.
Tonight we listened attentively to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). It was interesting to note that he continually condemned the opposition for lack of a program as an alternative to that proposed by the government. It is the responsibility of the government to propose policies that will correct the problems we face. It is all right for the Minister of Finance to try to lay blame on the opposition, but I point out that when the votes were counted in the last election and the Prime Minister received the support of the majority of representatives in this House, he immediately assumed the responsibility for initiating programs and policies necessary to strengthen the country. The responsibility of the opposition is to criticize and to effect constructive improvements to these policies and programs.
It is just not enough for the Minister of Finance to take the low-keyed approach that he took tonight, saying that our greatest problem is inflation and that the government must control it. There are scores of other problems pressing upon us which, unless they

The Address-Mr. Thompson are solved, will result in it not mattering whether or not we succeed with the problem of inflation. What we need, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) stated so well, is a Throne Speech that will be an agenda for action on the one hand and at the same time will be a strong expression of federal government concern regarding the nation's problems, particularly those in relation to national unity.
The Speech from the Throne made an appeal to young people by referring to a proposal to drop the voting age to 18 years. However, it is of interest to note that this recommendation is to be studied by a standing committee. In fact, much of the Speech from the Throne disturbed me because from its tone it seemed that instead of a Prime Minister speaking to his people we heard the voice of one who sounded more like a president.
The approach taken by the Prime Minister during the parliamentary recess indicated that this institution is not held in the same respect and regard by him as that held by his predecessors. The Speech from the Throne is actually a speech from our monarch, but for the first time this Speech from the Throne failed to speak of the cabinet or the government as Her cabinet or Her ministers. The only mention of the monarch in it was with reference to her pending visit to Manitoba.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I only hope that the Prime Minister will take the advice of His Highness Prince Philip when he said that if the Canadian people decide the monarchy is no longer an acceptable and useful institution in Canadian life, it would be up to them to do something about it, but it should be done openly. If it is the intention of the Prime Minister to eliminate the role of the monarch in our system of government, I think he owes it to the Canadian people to come out and say so, instead of letting it gradually slip away in the hope that they will let it go by without too much comment or criticism.
Coming back, Mr. Speaker, to the lowering of the voting age, during the last ten years it has been my impression that the young people of Canada have not really been demanding that the voting age be lowered. In fact, there is very little pressure from the young people on this subject. I think it is a good thing to encourage young people to participate directly in the process of government.


The Address-Mr. Thompson However, 1 do not think there is going to be any radical change in voting patterns, because in the three western provinces which have taken the lead in this there has been no evidence of any basic change in the pattern of voting.
What our young people are really looking for, particularly from the right hon. gentleman who is our Prime Minister, is leadership that will inspire them for the years ahead when they replace us, with the knowledge that what is being done now is preserving and strengthening the nation of which we are all a part. I find it very difficult to accept the lukewarm, passive approach to the basic problems as expressed in the Speech from the Throne. I would remind the government that on every side there are problems facing us that must be dealt with. It is not good enough to say that we are going to call a federal-provincial conference some time in the future, or that there is going to be a white paper on this or that. It is essential that the government give some indication of how it intends to solve these problems.
We are told that by 1980, 80 per cent of the people of Canada will be living in metropolitan or urban communities. This illustrates the tremendous need for adjustment in the area of transportation alone. Something will have to be done that is far different, far more impressive than that which is being offered at the present time.
The Speech from the Throne mentioned that the housing target for the next five years is one billion new homes in Canada. That is a notable target and we would all accept it. But how can we reach a target of one billion new homes with interest rates as they are at the present time? In fact, it is impossible to expect that people will be able to purchase the homes they need, and should have, if the interest paid over an amortization period of 20 to 25 years is two or three times the value of the home itself. What has been said about that? Nothing.
It is one thing for the Prime Minister to say that it is an international problem and refer to monetary policies-and in this he must include the inflated cost of money-but it is not good enough simply to say that this is a situation which affects the whole world while we in Canada do nothing about it.
The Minister of Finance has stated, quite correctly, that we have had a sustained and continuing period of affluence and economic expansion over the last few years, but does

that necessarily mean inflation is inevitable? He also mentioned that with the exception of wheat our exports have increased in price during the past year. I suppose he would imply that this meets the increased cost of production. But let him not talk that way to the farmers of this country. They know it is not just wheat that is involved. As they face the problem of inflation, probably more acutely than any other group in the country, they know it is not just wheat that has gone down in price. All grains and cereals-even beef, at its present high level-are still below what they were in price a few years ago.
The crisis that today faces Canada's farming industry demands more immediate and determined action than we have seen up to the present time. In fact, with a good deal of the western harvest already under snow and with little hope of its being taken off this fall, the crises that have developed in the west during the last few months have become more acute. I would like to think that the Speech from the Throne carried some word of encouragement for the farmers, but there was nothing in it.
I say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and those involved with policies relating to the sale of agricultural produce that we are not just facing a depression in western Canada today-we are in it already. A situation that has been difficult will inevitably become more difficult. This situation will not go away by itself. There is nothing in the Speech from the Throne for western farmers or eastern farmers, either.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is no easy solution to this problem but I do not accept the criticism from the government benches that we on the opposition side are just out to destroy or oppose those positive things they might suggest. Neither do we wish to encourage or incite the government to spend vast sums of money which are not readily available. Nevertheless, the problems are there.
The Speech from the Throne said something about the pollution of air and water. We know this is a tremendous problem, but it is no solution to say that in the future there will be a white paper on this matter, or that a federal-provincial conference will be called. It is imperative that some indication be given on how this problem will be dealt with by the federal government.
As I gauge the reaction of the Canadian people to the Speech from the Throne there is not very much optimism for the future as it


relates to the hard facts of life, and particularly to the economy. We are told that the white paper on tax reform will be available in about ten days, but unless it contains positive proposals to encourage the development of our own resources and to expand the productivity of this nation we are only talking to the wind. This is an area where the responsibility of government falls directly upon the Prime Minister and his cabinet. The Minister of Finance should talk more about what inflation actually is and how imperative it is that the productivity of this nation be speeded up to catch up with the tremendous overhead that the cost of government represents in this country. Today, with inflation pressing in on us, we are paying for the sins of governmental policy of the last five years. The cost of governing has gone up much faster than the increase in the growth of productivity. We have heard the CBC mentioned as an example. I would remind the House that last year the total expenditure of the CBC was more than $196 million.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
It would seem that there are ways in which this type of expenditure can be reduced. I am opposed to the abolition of the CBC, but we cannot afford the type of luxury involved in this tremendous expenditure of public funds. Similar charges could be repeated over and over again as one looks at policies of government expenditure and investment that have been carried on during the past five years. We need policies that will encourage the growth and development of this country and give us time to catch up with the growth of overhead costs incurred in financing the government of the country. That brings me to a point on which I wish to spend a few minutes. It concerns a policy that was implemented during the summer recess. It has been talked about but not really discussed in depth, and was touched on in the closing weeks of the previous session. I am speaking of the industrial incentive program announced in August.
The government has expressed concern over regional disparities in Canada. Unemployment, wages and costs, standards of community service, and consequently standards of living vary considerably in different regions of the country. In fact, as one crosses the breadth of Canada one sees that the differences between our regions divide us more from one another than do the differences that exist between us and our U.S. neighbour from

The Address-Mr. Thompson north to south. It is this factor that makes the governing of our country so difficult for any government. The federal government has recognized the problem that exists and has designated certain regions of Canada. In fact, there is one of these areas in every province, beaause all provinces have areas which the government considers to be most in need of stimulus and improvement. The government will grant substantial funds for capital investment to any manufacturing industry located in one of these designated regions. It will also make a grant for new jobs that are created.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the incentive program can not be expected to be a significant stimulus for new industries to establish in an area in which they otherwise would not have become established. As explained by government spokesmen, the incentive program is intended to be an incentive to industries which are planning to establish new plants, or to diversify into manufacturing new products, to locate in a designated area instead of some other area. It is therefore just as important for us to know where such industries will be attracted from as to define the areas to which they are to be induced to move. In other words, the program is a "have and have not" program in that every community is either labelled as one into which industry is to be encouraged to locate or as one from which industry should be diverted. Obviously, the economic health of the various regions of Canada ranges all the way from white to black through every shade of gray; and this black or white approach will in my opinion create serious discriminatory and inequitable situations.
In my constituency we do not expect any program of industrial incentives. For the most part the economic health of industries in central Alberta is good. I am concerned about the type of policy that will be developed in this incentive program, under which communities that are not in the hot or incentive areas will be forced to cool off. Indeed, the incentive program will draw industries away from the areas which are developing and place them in areas where it is to the manufacturer's benefit to locate.
I think it is accepted by all that the major urban centres of population, areas which are known as the hot areas of the country, are natural magnets for industry. They have built-in markets, transportation systems, pools of skilled labour and ancillary specialized services. On the other hand, labour is more expensive, more unionized and less stable;

Nevertheless, some industries are still able to locate outside metropolitan areas. Some are obliged to do so because of the nature of the industry. These are the "fall out" industries and they are the only industries that will move from one place to another if encouraged to do so by the incentive program. We are not, therefore, really talking about the over-all industrial picture of Canada; we are talking about a small proportion of industry which might be affected by this incentive program. You cannot describe such industry with any black or white label.
The smaller cities are fiercely competitive for these fall out industries, and it does not seem unreasonable to assume that the industrial location incentive plan will receive the most careful consideration of all fall-out industries. I would have thought, however, that the government could have come up with an incentive program that is not tax supported. Incentives in the form of concessions could have been given. Those incentives could have taken the form of tax allowances to encourage industries to locate in areas according to need.
I submit that for the government to say a certain area must be classified as an incentive area is the wrong way to approach the problem. The net result will be that we will worsen the situation and make it more difficult for areas, which at present are able to carry on by themselves, to carry on in future because under the new incentive program they will be discriminated against. I would have thought the government could have introduced a program which would have placed a premium on new industries being established in the "cool off" areas so as to balance the incentive of the hot areas. There could be direct and positive assistance other than direct subsidies to industries which wish to locate in areas not covered by the over-all incentive program as outlined by present governmental policy.
It seems to me that in trying to encourage industry to locate in various areas of the country we must develop a national viewpoint as opposed to a merely regional viewpoint. It is therefore obvious that the present type of program will make it increasingly difficult for those areas outside the incentive program, and which are not part of the industrial and urbanized hot areas, to compete with those areas which are to be given incentive assistance.

We have heard examples of the type of program the government ought to consider, and it would do well to listen to suggestions coming from this side of the house. It should not condemn our suggestions as being frivolous and merely aimed at bringing about increased expenditures in an attempt to solve our problems.

speechtext:
We face many other problems in Canada. We commend the Prime Minister for his attitude toward some of the problems which affect national unity. National unity does not depend on just cultural or political differences. It does not just depend on the solution of language difficulties. National unity will come about when the over-all economic and social development of this country is dealt with in an equitable way so that we may develop our tremendous reserve of resources, physical and human. At the same time there must be the type of government that will suit our needs. Our government must work for the national good. Canadians must not be burdened down with bureaucracy and the high cost associated with it. Essential projects must not be discarded because of government policies.
As we look at the coming months, at the legislation on the order paper and at the problems that involve us all, we can only hope that this session will be profitable. I encourage hon. members on the government side to study the proposals put forward by the Prime Minister in the Speech from the Throne and then to stand according to their convictions. Unless we come to grips with the basic problems affecting the over-all welfare of our country we shall not meet our responsibilities as we ought to meet them.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is to this end, Mr. Speaker, that we extend congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Speech from the Throne and to the new cabinet members. We trust this session of parliament will be worth while as far as the developing and unifying of our nation is concerned.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to join with previous speakers and congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the throne speech, the honourable members for Sarnia and Lapointe (Messrs. Cullen and Marceau).


They certainly did a good job and I am pleased to see once again that the present government is made up of qualified men.
I would also like to pay tribute to three great men who sat in this house before me: senator Hurtubise and Leoda Gauthier, both deceased, and judge Odias Godin who sat in the house between 1958 and 1965 and who is present in the house this evening.
Mr. Speaker, these three remarkable men have left their mark not only on my region but throughout the country.
In the next few minutes, I shall try to give my impression on the contents of the throne speech. Then, I shall do my best to draw the attention of the house to problems peculiar to my riding of Nickel Belt and to Northern Ontario. Finally, I intend to inform the government about representations by the people whom I have the honour and pleasure of representing.
Mr. Speaker, I would not forgive myself if I failed to congratulate the right honourable Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for his sense of realism, his clearsightedness, his devotion and his courage since he came to power. Under his leadership, the government of this country is achieving gradually the just society which it proposed to establish.
Indeed, his philosophy of the just society emerges with a greater clarity and vigour in the speech from the throne. When reading carefully that document which sets forth a program much more personal, concrete and specific for this second session, one realizes that it contains a sound philosophy for the country, a philosophy designed to show a growing difference towards the individual, to define the public weal above all in relation to the improvement in the well-being, the security and the freedom of each individual.
Last year, after having succeeded in laying the foundations of a just society through the reform of parliamentary procedure, the government now proposes, in this second session, to really set itself to work by introducing bills designed to do justice to Canadian citizens.
One has only to review some of the most important legislative measures which will be proposed in the second session to realize that the government is firmly determined to pay more attention to our people who are in less fortunate conditions than the rest of the country.
Like my constituents, I am pleased that the government is establishing programs to reduce economic regional disparity and to
The Address-Mr. Serre further protect the rights of individuals and minorities.
Here are a few examples: it will give special attention to the necessity of employment surveys among Canadians of Indian descent. It intends to vote an increased budget for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which becomes the main instrument in the fight against social and economic disparities. Some of the measures are the guarantee of liguistic rights and programs of assistance for minorities; a tax reform aimed at establishing a new formula for a fairer distribution of the tax burden; a complete revision of the policy on social security; amendments to the legislation governing labor-management relations; new Criminal Code amendments to provide better protection of individuals' rights; and special attention to housing problems.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that despite the threat of inflation the government's objective is to construct, over a period of five years, one million new housing units to meet the needs of low-income families.
The government will also propose measures to eradicate water pollution, a revision of the legislation regarding consumer goods in order to give consumers a better protection and a thorough reform of the unemployment insurance plan to make benefits available to a greater number of unemployed.
Under the heading of reforms affecting the rights of individuals, I am very happy to find that the government intends to lower the voting age to 18. The young people from my riding know that I have been working for a long time towards that goal. Mr. Speaker, I am not one of those who entertain doubts and misgivings about the ability of the younger generation to take those new responsibilities.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
On the contrary, I have always had great confidence in youth. Since I am one of the youngest members of this house, and a professor, I can say from personal experience that today's youth is much more mature and better informed about politics than previous generations and, in many cases, in a much better position to exercise its right to vote than a certain class of adults.
I say: Let us have no fear of giving responsibilities to our young people. They will protest less and bring a most valuable contribution to their environment and to our country.
In my riding, there are already a significant number of young people of 16, 17 and 18


The Address-Mr. Serri years of age who are very actively engaged in politics and who could teach a great deal to their elders. They are undoubtedly a great source of inspiration in their own circle.
I am convinced that this change of attitude in the federal policy will encourage a growing number of young people to take more interest in State affairs.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the population of the Nickel Belt constituency, the large constituency, which I have the honour to represent in this house, looks favourably upon the new measures considered by the government at the beginning of this second session, and I am sure my constituents are ready to support it. However, it is not all beer and skittles in Nickel Belt and Northern Ontario. We have to face a lot of specific problems that go back a long way; some of them are becoming so acute that they call for immediate action from the governments.
The most serious problem in my region is unquestionably air and water pollution'. This problem has been rampant for several years and the situation is getting worse and worse instead of getting better.
Last Friday the Toronto Telegram published an article entitled: Sudbury: devastation total. The disastrous situation in which my region is plunged is fairly well analysed there. My constituents are getting very impatient at the government inaction about it. They do not intend to remain passive any longer. They are well determined to take the necessary steps and invite the government to act immediately. The continuing effort of a citizen committee from Sudbury and the area, under the skilful leadership of Mr. Paul Falkowski, deserves certainly to be pointed out here.
Mr. Speaker, either according to tradition or to the constitution, it has always been recognized that pollution was a provincial field of jurisdiction. However, since it has become apparent that the provincial government has been unable to find solutions to control pollution, my fellow-citizens as well as myself are urging the federal government to intervene.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Since this problem is quite extensive in- the Sudbury area, a research centre to help the corporations to find some means to control pollution should be established as soon as possible.
[Mr. Serrfi.l
My constituents will certainly be more reassured if they note that the federal government is now determined to take the initiative by introducing during this second session a new bill aimed at preventing water pollution.
The housing crisis is quite acute in my constituency as the result of a lack of funds. The government will have to give its immediate attention to that problem by finding means to provide funds at more reasonable rates of interest to people with low incomes.
I strongly hope that the government will seriously consider the possibility of withdrawing the 11 per cent tax on building materials, at least for individuals who wish to build their own homes. I especially hope that the provincial authorities will stop blaming Ottawa and that they will assume their responsibilities in that field by providing the municipalities with the water, sewage and planning services they need.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I can hardly understand that such a corporation as the CBC which is entirely subsidized by the citizens is left so free to broadcast what it likes without having to answer for it to the people. I suggest that this situation is completely abnormal, and that we, as the elected representatives of the people, should be able to exercise greater control. My constituents are stirred up, and rightfully so, because of certain programs that have a very bad influence on the people of this country.
The sole effect of many programs is to lower the moral standards. There are, of course, many good programs, but more effort should be put, I think, into attempting to present a greater number of educational and cultural ones.
The people of northern Ontario were very happy to learn of the introduction by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion of a program of subsidies to secondary industries. It will surely help to reduce the poverty and unemployment that exist presently in many sectors of my district and in the whole of northern Ontario.
I believe, however, that this new program, like similar ones in the past, is of benefit only to certain selected groups and to certain more-favoured sectors, at the expense of the poor and of the less-favoured regions. For that reason, I have invited the municipal authorities in my riding to take it upon themselves to establish the structures liable to


attract industries to their localities. Many municipalities have already responded and have created industrial committees, and for this I congratulate them.
I am sure they will receive all the necessary co-operation from the various government agencies. I have already repeatedly stressed in the house the need for secondary industries in northern Ontario. There is no need for me to belabour the point now. May I simply enumerate the types of industries that more than any others would be of benefit to the economy of my region.
Plants for machine assembling and construction of mining equipment could be established, a local slaughtering house with an inspector on permanent duty in order to encourage the raising of cattle, a local warehouse for agricultural products, increased assistance to the farmers who are now forced to leave their farms on account of lack of facilities, in order to allow them to compete with the other centres of the province and the country.
Special attention should be given to the tourist industry. It is known that in northern Ontario natural resources and scenic beauties are diverse and plentiful. For example, I hope that the federal government will consider the possibility of developing a national park in that part of my constituency which is called French River. As is well known, this region has a rich historical past. It was the road followed in days of yore by Champlain, the first missionaries and the first settlers who developed northern Ontario.
Many other types of industries could prosper in my constituency. In order to ensure a proper development of this vast region, I feel that a socio-economical study should be undertaken by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
Such a study would promote a better coordination of local efforts and better planning.
My French-speaking compatriots in Ontario are greatly pleased by the determination of the present government in its efforts to ensure linguistic equality in the federal government's agencies, and wherever it is warranted by the population breakdown.
Franco-Ontarians are following very closely the efforts of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) who is devising an assistance program for French-speaking minorities, aiming not only at ensuring their survival but mainly at enabling them to develop fully within the Francophone and Canadian frameworks.
The Address-Mr. Serre
Having conducted for several years their struggle for survival, and their fight is certainly bearing fruit, if we consider that nearly three quarters of a million French-speaking Canadians live in Ontario, the biggest concentration being in the Nickel Belt area, in northern Ontario, my French-speaking compatriots now see more reason for hope in the new policy of the federal government and in the change of attitude of the provincial government who has just granted French secondary schools to the French-speaking population.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Such commendable initiatives certainly deserve our admiration and all our gratitude.
However, now that we are guaranteed linguistic equality under the law, we must not stop there. The French-speaking people of Ontario recognize, as does the Secretary of State, indeed, that bilingualism will be shortlived if it is not founded on cultural bases which immerge us in tradition and provide us with a sense of evolution.
At the priority level, we need, therefore, some cultural stimulation. The French-speaking people in Ontario have at their disposal few French cultural services and the existing ones are often inferior to the valuable English cultural services or less interesting.
Prompted by a strong desire for perfection and self-achievement, in order to participate on an equal footing with their English-speaking fellow-citizens, in the building of a united country, my constituents, like myself, urgently demand that the federal government designate as a bilingual district the Sudbury area; that subsidies be granted to various social and cultural services, that the C.B.C. establish as soon as possible in Sudbury a French television station with a local production centre responsible for Ontario public affairs and the development of local talents.
They also ask that additional financial assistance be granted to French newspapers. Special attention should, for instance, be given to the only French weekly in the Sudbury region, Le Voyageur, a local undertaking which certainly deserves recognition; but which is having a hard time to subsist due to lack of money. They want additional grants for the Laurentienne University of Sudbury to promote cultural activities and retraining courses to be made more easily available to the French population by providing French courses in Sudbury.


The Address-Mr. Serre
I already know, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State and the government will find the necessary means to comply with those legitimate requests from my fellow-citizens of northern Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to represent a most diversified population. The Nickel Belt riding and the Sudbury region are populated with men and women of all possible nationalities, with the most varied cultural background. The valuable cultural contribution from all these various ethnic groups, and I have particularly in mind the Ukrainians, the Italians, the Germans and the Finnish people, to mention just a few, is certainly the greatest resource of my region. The extraordinary thing is that despite this mosaic of races, religions, languages and cultures, we have learned to live together, growing and mutually enriching each other in perfect harmony.
We have really achieved unity in diversity. That is why I don't hesitate to offer my region as a model for the whole country. I would even go as far as to assert that the future of Confederation will be decided in Northern Ontario. In that sense we are perhaps twenty years ahead of the other parts of the country. Indeed my region already gives a true picture of what Canada could be tomorrow.
Now I would like to challenge certain extremists of the province of Quebec, including Mr. Levesque, who have no faith in the country's future and I would like to invite them to climb down from their ivory tower and to spend some time in my region. They would certainly find it a beneficial source of inspiration.

Mr. Speaker, I want to move to a more progressive and effective session. I hope my constituents will continue to give me their support, their recommendations and their most valuable suggestions so that with them, together with all members on all sides of the house, we can work for the common good of our great country, Canada.
